books.title: The Steam Engine
books.art_why: Historical invention from the 1700s-1800s; early machines and events are best shown as drawings.

pages.text: The Steam Engine will take you on a ride through history to introduce you to one of the world’s most important inventions. You will learn how a steam engine works, who invented the early ones, and how steam engines changed the way people and goods were.
pages.brief: A steam engine appears at the center of a journey through history. Around it, simple scenes suggest early inventors, a boiler making steam, a locomotive, a steamboat, factory machines and a modern power plant, showing how one invention connects past and present.

pages.text: An Invention That Changed the World For thousands of years, people used their muscles for work. They also used animals to help them. In the 1700s, the invention of the steam engine changed everything. People began to make fewer goods by hand. Instead, they used machines. Many of those machines were powered by steam.
pages.brief: For thousands of years, people use their muscles and animals for work. In the 1700s, a steam engine changes everything: people make fewer goods by hand and use machines instead. Many machines are powered by steam in workshops or early factories.

pages.text: What Is Steam? Have you ever watched someone boil water in a pot on the stove? Sometimes you can see a little cloud above the pot. That’s steam. It can only be seen when it hits cooler air. Steam is a gas. People make steam do work by boiling water. They heat up the water in a gigantic pot called a boiler. They make the boiler hot by burning fuel, such as coal. Burning coal becomes hotter than the top of a stove—a lot hotter! The heat boils the water and makes steam. Steam takes up more room than liquid water. As the steam expands, it pushes the moveable parts of a machine. The movement of those parts creates power.
pages.brief: A person watches a pot of water boiling on a stove, and a little cloud of steam rises above it. In a large boiler, fuel such as coal burns hot, heating water until steam forms. The expanding steam pushes moveable parts of a machine, creating power.

pages.text: The First Real Steam Engines Almost 300 years ago, in 1712, Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine. Others had built steam engines, but Newcomen’s was the first to work really well. He used his steam engine to run a water pump, which pumped water out of coal mines. Miners could then reach more coal. The engine had one problem. It needed a large amount of coal to do a small amount of work.
pages.brief: In 1712, Thomas Newcomen stands beside his steam engine at a coal mine. The engine runs a water pump that lifts water out of the mine so miners can reach more coal. The machine is useful but needs a large amount of coal to do a small amount of work.

pages.text: Steam Engine Improvements In the 1760s, Scotsman James Watt improved Newcomen’s engine. He made the machine work with less coal. Watt also made other kinds of steam engines. He made one called the rotary (circular) steam engine. It could run all kinds of machines. This invention was one event that led to the Industrial Revolution, also known as the Age of Steam. The Age of Steam brought new ways to do work and new ways for people and goods to travel.
pages.brief: Scotsman James Watt works on an improved steam engine in the 1760s, using less coal than Newcomen’s engine. He also builds a rotary steam engine that can run all kinds of machines. Around him, the Industrial Revolution, or Age of Steam, brings new ways to work and travel.

pages.text: High-Pressure Steam Engines At the beginning of the Age of Steam, Watt’s steam engines used low- pressure steam. His steam engines were big, and they operated, or worked, slowly. Watt knew he could make smaller and faster steam engines. But he would have to use higher-pressure steam. He was against that idea. Higher pressure could cause a boiler to explode. An explosion could injure or kill people.
pages.brief: James Watt stands beside a large, slow low-pressure steam engine. He knows smaller, faster engines would need higher-pressure steam, but he is against the idea. He warns that higher pressure could make a boiler explode and injure or kill people.

pages.text: Many inventors saw the danger of high- pressure steam. They built high-pressure steam engines anyway. They thought that smaller engines could be used to do more things. In the early 1800s, Richard Trevithick (trev-ITH-ik) built a high-pressure steam engine in England. High-pressure steam engines soon became common. They could be used to power trains.
pages.brief: Many inventors understand the danger of high-pressure steam but build high-pressure steam engines anyway. In the early 1800s in England, Richard Trevithick builds one. Soon high-pressure steam engines become common, and they can be used to power trains.

pages.text: Steam-Powered Transportation Trevithick built one of the first steam locomotives, or trains, in 1804. It hauled coal at a factory. Other people also built train engines. Soon these engines were pulling long lines of cars with passengers or goods. Steam engines helped railroads spread across the world.
pages.brief: In 1804, Richard Trevithick builds one of the first steam locomotives. It hauls coal at a factory. Other people build train engines too, and soon long lines of cars carrying passengers or goods are pulled by steam. Steam engines help railroads spread across the world.

pages.text: In the early 1800s, ships also began to use steam. Some sailed on the oceans. New Yorker Robert Fulton built the first moneymaking river steamboat in 1807. By the mid-1800s, beautiful steamboats traveled up and down American rivers. River steamboats presented the danger that James Watt had warned about. Steam explosions sometimes happened with locomotives, but they were common with steamboats. Many people were injured or killed in steamboat accidents.
pages.brief: In the early 1800s, ships begin to use steam. Robert Fulton, a New Yorker, builds the first moneymaking river steamboat in 1807. By the mid-1800s, beautiful steamboats travel up and down American rivers. Steam explosions sometimes happen, especially on steamboats, injuring or killing many people.

pages.text: One of the worst disasters in American history took place on April 27, 1865. The boiler on the crowded steamboat Sultana exploded. The ship burned. More than 1,700 people died.
pages.brief: On April 27, 1865, the crowded steamboat Sultana is on a river when its boiler explodes. The ship burns. More than 1,700 people die in one of the worst disasters in American history. The scene shows the damaged steamboat and the fire.

pages.text: The Age of Steam Draws to a Close By the early 1900s, people had found ways to replace steam power. In factories, electricity now ran most machines. Electric engines did not produce steam or smoke. Electric engines made subways and streetcars easy for everyday use. It became easier to travel around a city. The diesel engine also doomed the steam engine. It ran better and could go farther faster. Steam locomotives ran in the United States until the 1960s. By then, almost all locomotives had diesel engines.
pages.brief: By the early 1900s, electric engines run most factory machines, producing no steam or smoke. Electric engines make subways and streetcars easy for everyday city travel. The diesel engine also replaces steam because it runs better and goes farther faster. Steam locomotives continue in the United States until the 1960s.

pages.text: Modern Uses of Steam Although the Age of Steam is long over, steam is still important. For plants use it to produce electricity. It powers your lights and your television. pages.brief: A modern power plant burns coal to make steam and produce electricity. Nearby, a water heater, an electric stove, a television and lights show everyday uses of that power, with piles of coal suggesting how much fuel a single household needs.

pages.text: Some people believe there is still a need for steam power. Steam power, they say, costs less than diesel fuel for trains. Steam power can also be generated using solar panels, which do not use fossil fuels like coal to make electricity. That makes steam power better for the environment than it is now. Steam power is useful and will probably have a place in the modern world.
pages.brief: Some people believe steam power is still needed. They say steam costs less than diesel fuel for trains. Steam power can also be generated using solar panels, which do not use fossil fuels like coal, making it better for the environment. Steam power is useful and probably has a place in the modern world.

books.title: Summer Olympic Events
books.art_why: Modern Olympic athletes, sports and stadiums exist today and are widely photographed.

pages.text: The Olympic Games began over one hundred years ago as a way to feature the best athletes from around the.
pages.brief: A group of athletes from different countries stand together in a packed Olympic stadium, smiling and shaking hands. The scene suggests friendship and understanding among people from around the world as they meet at the Games.

pages.text: The Summer Olympic Games The modern Summer Olympic Games began in 1894. They were inspired by athletic competitions held in ancient Greece. The Games are intended to promote understanding and friendship among people from all countries. The Summer Olympics are held every four years. Each Olympics is held in a different city around the world. Athletes compete in hundreds of events. They try their best to win gold, silver, or bronze medals for their home countries. pages.brief: Athletes from many countries compete in a packed modern Olympic stadium, running, jumping and throwing. At the side, a podium holds gold, silver and bronze medals. The scene shows the Summer Games, held every four years in a different city around the world.

pages.text: The Olympic Torch The Summer Olympics start with an opening ceremony. The ceremony usually includes a parade of the athletes. An important part of the ceremony is the lighting of the Olympic flame by a person carrying the Olympic torch.
pages.brief: In a packed Olympic stadium, athletes parade during the opening ceremony. A torchbearer carries the Olympic torch toward a large cauldron and uses it to light the Olympic flame, while spectators watch from the stands.

pages.text: The torch is lit in Greece several months before the start of the games. It is then carried to the host city by a series of runners. It arrives at the Olympic stadium on the opening day of the games. By this time, it has been handed off from one runner to the next many times during its long journey. At the opening ceremony, the final runner enters the stadium carrying the torch. They use it to light the Olympic flame. The Olympic flame burns throughout the Olympics. It is not put out until the closing ceremony.
pages.brief: A series of runners carry the Olympic torch across roads and countryside, handing the flame from one to the next. In the foreground, the final runner enters a packed Olympic stadium carrying the torch and lights the Olympic flame, which burns in a large cauldron until the closing ceremony.

pages.text: Events The Summer Games include team sports such as basketball, soccer, volleyball, and field hockey. They also include many individual events. Let’s look at some of the events.
pages.brief: Athletes play team sports in an Olympic stadium: basketball players shoot at a hoop, soccer players chase a ball, volleyball players leap at the net, and field hockey players swing sticks. Nearby, individual athletes train and compete alone.

pages.text: Water Sports Water sports include water polo, diving, and swimming. Some of the swimming races are short, and swimmers swim only two lengths of the pool. Other races are longer. They sometimes include more than one swimmer in a relay.
pages.brief: In a large Olympic swimming pool, swimmers race in short and long events; one swimmer touches the wall after two lengths while others swim a longer distance. At one end, water polo players pass a ball, and a diver stands on a high board above the water.

pages.text: Many swimming races allow swimmers to use only one kind of stroke. But in the freestyle event, swimmers can choose the stroke they want to use. The breaststroke, backstroke, and the butterfly are all used in different races.
pages.brief: Several swimmers cross a blue Olympic pool using different strokes: one swims breaststroke, one backstroke, one butterfly, and one freestyle. Their arms and legs move in distinct ways as they race toward the pool wall, each in their own lane.

pages.text: In diving events, divers jump from high above the water. Divers do twists, flips, and turns while in the air. They get points for the difficulty of the dive and how small a splash they make when they hit the water.
pages.brief: A diver leaps from a high platform above a pool, twisting and flipping in the air with arms and legs tucked. The diver aims for a tiny splash as they enter the water, showing the difficulty of the dive.

pages.text: Track and Field Track and field events include running, throwing, and jumping competitions. The marathon is the longest running event. It is over 42 kilometers (26 mi) long. The shortest races are called dashes.
pages.brief: On a track and field arena, distance runners stride through a long marathon course while sprinters explode from the starting line in a short dash. Nearby, athletes prepare to throw and jump, showing running, throwing and jumping competitions.

pages.text: Runners often train for the Olympic Games by running in locations high in the mountains. This training helps their bodies become better at delivering oxygen to their muscles to create energy.
pages.brief: High in the mountains, runners train along winding roads with thin air. Their faces show effort as they breathe deeply, building their bodies’ ability to deliver oxygen to their muscles and create energy for Olympic races.

pages.text: In throwing events, the objective is to throw a hammer, discus, javelin, or shot put as far as possible. Athletes competing in these events must be very strong.
pages.brief: Strong athletes stand in a throwing circle and hurl a hammer, discus, javelin and shot put as far as they can. Their muscles strain with effort, and the heavy objects sail through the air over a marked field.

pages.text: In jumping events, athletes are judged on the height or distance of their jumps. In the high jump, athletes leap over a bar. The bar is raised higher until only one person can jump it. In the long jump, athletes leap as far as they can. In the pole vault, athletes use a pole to help them leap over a very high bar.
pages.brief: Athletes compete in jumping events: one leaps over a high-jump bar that rises higher and higher, another sprints and launches into a long jump, and a third uses a pole to vault over a very high bar. Each tries to reach the greatest height or distance.

pages.text: Gymnastics Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl through the air. They demonstrate their timing, balance, flexibility, strength, and skill. Some popular events include the rings, balance beam and the pommel horse. In the balance beam event, they must turn and flip on the narrow beam.
pages.brief: Gymnasts leap, flip and twirl through the air in a bright arena. One balances on a narrow beam, turning and flipping; another swings on the rings; another works on the pommel horse. Their timing, balance, flexibility, strength and skill are on display.

pages.text: Fencing Olympic fencers duel with practice swords. They score points by touching their opponents with their swords on different parts of the body. Fencers wear protective masks and clothing and use special swords so that the competition is safe. Fencers are allowed to move forward and backward as they fight, but they can only move a little from side to side. Fencers use three different kinds of swords.
pages.brief: Two fencers wear protective masks and white clothing as they duel with practice swords. They move forward and backward, lunging to touch each other on different parts of the body, while staying only a little apart from side to side. Three different swords rest nearby.

pages.text: Pentathlon One event created specifically for the Olympics is the pentathlon. The founder of the modern Games, Baron Pierre de Coubertin, created this event. He was inspired by the pentathlon in the Ancient Olympics. The name pentathlon comes from the Greek words for five and contest.
pages.brief: Baron Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Games, stands thoughtfully beside an ancient Greek athlete and a modern pentathlete. The scene links the ancient pentathlon to the new Olympic event, whose name comes from the Greek words for five and contest.

pages.text: The pentathlon is based on an imaginary scenario of a soldier who is trapped behind enemy lines. The athlete must ride a horse, shoot targets with a pistol, fight with a sword, run, and swim. The competitor with the best total score in all five events wins. Both men and women compete in the pentathlon.
pages.brief: An athlete imagines being a soldier trapped behind enemy lines: they ride a horse, shoot at targets with a pistol, fight with a sword, run across rough ground and swim through water. Men and women compete in all five events, and the best total score wins.

pages.text: Event Categories The Summer Olympics include more than thirty sports with hundreds of events. More events can be added at every Olympics. books.title: Sonia Sotomayor Joins the Supreme Court
books.art_why: It is about a named famous person, Sonia Sotomayor.

pages.text: The first Hispanic female Supreme Court justice, Sonia Sotomayor, is an American role model. She has set new standards for what women can do and achieve in the world and is proof that hard work and belief in oneself can help a person overcome any obstacle. This.
pages.brief: Sonia Sotomayor, the first Hispanic female Supreme Court justice, stands as an American role model. She looks confident, showing that women can set new standards and achieve great things through hard work and belief in themselves.

pages.text: A Big Dream When she was a young girl, Sonia Sotomayor dreamed of becoming a detective. Doctors told her when she was eight that she had Type 1 diabetes. It was a big change. Sonia had to learn to take good care of herself because this is a serious condition. Sonia’s dreams also changed. She wanted to become a lawyer.
pages.brief: Young Sonia Sotomayor dreams of becoming a detective. When she is eight, doctors tell her she has Type 1 diabetes, and she learns to take good care of herself. Her dream changes, and she now wants to become a lawyer.

pages.text: Sonia’s parents had moved to New York from Puerto Rico. Sonia’s father died when she was nine. Her mother worked hard to support Sonia and her brother. Sonia tried to be the best student she could be. She studied, made good grades, and won many awards. She won scholarships, or money for school, to attend Princeton University and then Yale Law School. She was an excellent student at both schools.
pages.brief: Sonia’s parents moved from Puerto Rico to New York, and her father died when she was nine. Her mother works hard to support Sonia and her brother. Sonia studies, makes good grades, wins awards, and earns scholarships to Princeton University and Yale Law School.

pages.text: The Dream Comes True After graduating from law school, Sotomayor got her first job as a lawyer. Her dream had come true. After several years as a lawyer, her dream changed again. She wanted to become a judge. Her dream came true in 1991.
pages.brief: After graduating from law school, Sonia Sotomayor gets her first job as a lawyer, and her dream comes true. After several years as a lawyer, she wants to become a judge. Her dream comes true in 1991.

pages.text: In May 2009, President Barack Obama had to choose a new justice for the U.S. Supreme Court. One of the justices, David H. Souter, was retiring. The president Judge Sotomayor was his choice to Souter. The president said she had done a great job as a judge and would be a wise justice. Do You Know? Justices of the U.S. Supreme Court are very important. They decide if laws follow the U.S. Constitution. The Constitution is the country’s set of rules and laws that protect our rights. The nine justices of the Supreme Court make decisions that affect many people.
pages.brief: In May 2009, President Barack Obama chooses Judge Sonia Sotomayor for the U.S. Supreme Court after Justice David H. Souter retires. The president says she has done a great job as a judge. Nine justices decide whether laws follow the U.S. Constitution.

pages.text: Picking a New Justice Presidents often choose a justice who agrees with them on important ideas. All U.S. Supreme Court justices have worked as lawyers. Many justices have not been judges in other courts, as Sotomayor has. A justice can be any age. The youngest justice was thirty-two when chosen. The oldest was sixty-five. Presidents often choose a younger person so he or she can work on the court for many years. Sotomayor was fifty-five when President Obama chose her.
pages.brief: President Obama considers a new Supreme Court justice. All justices have worked as lawyers, and many have not been judges in other courts. Justices can be any age; the youngest was thirty-two and the oldest sixty-five. Sotomayor is fifty-five when he chooses her.

pages.text: The Supreme Court is over two old. For most of that time, all of the justices on the court have been white men. Yet the justices make decisions that affect all kinds of people in different areas of the country. Some presidents now try to make the court more representative of the country. Thurgood Marshall joined the court as its first Black justice in 1967. Sandra Day O’Connor joined the court as its first female justice in 1981.
pages.brief: The U.S. Supreme Court is shown as an old institution, over two hundred years old. For most of that time, all its justices have been white men. Thurgood Marshall becomes the first Black justice in 1967, and Sandra Day O’Connor becomes the first female justice in 1981.

pages.text: Finding the Right Person President Obama, like other presidents before him, asked for help to find the best justice. Lawyers and advisers to the president made a list of people who would make good justices. They checked to make sure the people on the list were fair and followed the law. Sonia Sotomayor was on the list. She had been a lawyer and judge for many years. She would be the third woman ever to be a Supreme Court justice. Sotomayor would join Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the second woman on the court. Judge Sotomayor would be the first Latina and the first person with diabetes to be chosen as a justice.

Sonia Sotomayor is on the list after many years as a lawyer and judge. She would be the third woman justice, joining Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and the first Latina and first person with diabetes chosen.

pages.text: The Judiciary Committee A group of senators called the Judiciary Committee investigated Judge Sotomayor. She answered the senators’ questions about decisions she had made as a judge. She talked about things she had said in speeches. Judge Sotomayor explained how she would be fair when deciding cases in the future. The committee reported its findings to the rest of the Senate. pages.text: The Senate Votes Some people who disagreed with President Obama’s ideas also disagreed with choosing Judge Sotomayor. But when the Senate voted on August 6, 2009, the majority voted to confirm Judge Sotomayor. Two days later, Sonia Sotomayor took an oath, or made a promise, to follow the Constitution. She was now the 111th justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.

pages.text: The Job of the New Justice Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor has an office in the Supreme Court Building. She had to hire people to work in her office. She also had to learn the rules of the Supreme Court, just as you would learn the rules at a new school. Justice Sotomayor’s main job now is to listen to cases that are brought to the Supreme Court and make wise decisions.
pages.brief: Justice Sonia Sotomayor works in her office in the Supreme Court Building. She hires people to work in her office and learns the rules of the Supreme Court, just as a student learns rules at a new school. Her main job is to listen to cases and make wise decisions.

pages.text: Conclusion Justice Sotomayor has made many dreams in her life come true. Being a justice is a very important job. Most presidents only get to choose one or two Supreme Court justices during their time in office. It is a very important decision. Justice Sotomayor tries to be the best justice she can be. She helps make decisions that affect all Americans!
pages.brief: Justice Sonia Sotomayor sits in the Supreme Court, having made many dreams in her life come true. Being a justice is a very important job, and most presidents choose only one or two Supreme Court justices. She tries to be the best justice she can and helps make decisions that affect all Americans.

pages.text: In 2010, it happened again, fifteen blocks from the first hole. This time, the hole swallowed a three-story clothing factory and left another gaping chasm in a major intersection. Miraculously, no one was injured. Sinkholes happen all over the world, in the middle of cities and in the middle of nowhere. Though sinkholes take years to form, each time a new sinkhole opens up in the earth, it takes people by surprise. What Causes Sinkholes? The ground we stand on feels solid. Underground, however, a lot is happening. Water trickles and flows, slowly eroding rocks and soil. This creates underground spaces. These result in sinkholes. Sinkholes don’t happen just anywhere, though. Most natural sinkholes form where there are certain kinds of soft bedrock. Bedrock is a layer of underground rock. The ground above it and on the surface is called the overburden.
pages.brief: In a major intersection, a gaping chasm has opened fifteen blocks from an earlier hole. A three-story clothing factory has been swallowed, yet no one is injured. Below the solid-looking ground, water trickles through soft bedrock and soil, slowly eroding rocks and creating underground spaces.

pages.text: Rain or underground water drips and flows into this bedrock and erodes it. This creates open spaces such as underground caves or caverns. Over time, these spaces get bigger. Eventually, the overburden may slowly drop down to form a sinkhole. Sometimes, though, sinkholes can open suddenly and swallow buildings, cars, and people. Two Types There are two main types of sinkholes. The first is a cover-subsidence sinkhole ( subside means to sink or settle). A cover-subsidence sinkhole forms when water wears a space in the underground bedrock. The overburden above the bedrock then shifts downward. Most sinkholes of this kind form slowly and may measure only a few yards across. The overburden may contain a lot of sand that easily slides into the underground space. These sinkholes often create a bowl shape on the surface. They may become ponds or wetlands if water has no way to drain out.
pages.brief: Underground water drips and flows through bedrock, eroding open caves and caverns. Above, the overburden slowly shifts downward into a bowl shape, and sand slides into the underground space. At the surface, the sunken bowl may hold water and become a pond or wetland.

pages.text: This sinkhole forms when a space gets bigger and bigger under the surface. The overburden gets thinner as dirt, sand, and other sediment fall into the space. The ground around this kind of sinkhole may contain a lot of sticky clay. Clay helps hold the overburden together. Without warning, though, the surface may collapse into the underground space.
pages.brief: Beneath the surface, an underground space grows larger as dirt, sand, and sediment fall into it, thinning the overburden. Sticky clay in the ground helps hold the overburden together until, without warning, the surface collapses into the underground space.

pages.text: China’s Xiaozhai Tiankeng is considered the deepest sinkhole in the world. More than 2,165 feet (660 m) deep, this sinkhole could swallow a 200-story skyscraper. The Sarisarinama sinkholes in Venezuela were discovered in 1961. Scientists have discovered plants and animals inside that are found nowhere else. Sinkholes Caused by Humans Some sinkholes result from underground construction. In cities, tunnels and pipes crisscross under many buildings and streets. If those pipes get old and worn out, they can collapse, allowing liquid to escape and eat away at the ground. Eventually, the pavement caves in. Work crews must check these underground spaces regularly to make sure they are solid. If a sinkhole forms in a city it can do a lot of damage, as in Guatemala City, where leaking pipes may have triggered the gaping holes in the city streets.
pages.brief: China’s Xiaozhai Tiankeng plunges more than 2,165 feet, a sinkhole deep enough to swallow a 200-story skyscraper. In Venezuela, the Sarisarinama sinkholes, discovered in 1961, contain plants and animals inside that are found nowhere else.

pages.text: Underground mines can also cause sinkholes. Near one Russian city, underground water filled an old mine. The bedrock of salt began dissolving. In 1986, a huge sinkhole opened up. It grew to 780 feet (238 m) deep and covered more area than 25 football fields. It is still growing, and new sinkholes are opening up. Hundreds of people have had to leave their homes. To be safe, the entire city may need to move. Some geologists argue that holes caused by human activity shouldn’t be called sinkholes because true sinkholes result from natural processes. Garbage In, Garbage Out People sometimes treat sinkholes like garbage dumps. They will throw in junk, trash, even animal waste. This is a terrible idea. Many sinkholes drain into underground water sources. This is the same water that people drink. It is the to water their crops. The result is pollution in our food and drinking water.
pages.brief: Under city streets, worn pipes and tunnels crisscross beneath buildings; leaking liquid eats the ground until pavement caves in. Near a Russian city, water fills an old salt mine and a vast sinkhole grows, forcing people to leave their homes. Junk and trash dumped into a sinkhole pollute underground water.

pages.text: Dealing with Sinkholes Predicting where natural sinkholes will form is tricky. The erosion that creates them is usually hidden underground. The type of bedrock is the most important factor in whether or not sinkholes form. Areas with soft bedrock that also get heavy rains are at even greater risk. The rainwater adds weight to the overburden. The draining water can also speed up underground erosion. Where Sinkholes Sink N.
pages.brief: Underground erosion stays hidden as geologists predict where natural sinkholes may form. Soft bedrock is the most important factor; areas with soft bedrock and heavy rains face greater risk because rainwater adds weight to the overburden and draining water speeds underground erosion.

pages.text: Tilting trees or signposts can be early clues that the ground is shifting. Growing cracks in walls and sidewalks can also warn that a sinkhole is getting ready to cause trouble. If a sinkhole forms under a can pour tons of dirt and concrete into the hole. This is called grouting. The goal is to plug the hole. Sometimes, though, the dirt and concrete just disappear into the underground space. Another method uses steel rods. These long, strong rods are pushed into solid bedrock deep underground. The rods are then joined to the base of the house. This helps keep the building stable and safe.
pages.brief: Tilting trees and signposts and growing cracks in walls and sidewalks show the ground shifting. Under a house, workers pour tons of dirt and concrete into a sinkhole to plug it; long steel rods are pushed into solid bedrock and joined to the house’s base to keep it stable.

pages.text: Conclusion Sinkholes can be destructive, but they are rarely dangerous. In some places, they are even beautiful. In parts of Mexico, for instance, sinkholes form lovely pools full of cool, clean water. Sinkholes are also interesting to study. They show water’s powerful effects on soil and rock. Even on solid ground, amazing things are happening beneath our feet.
pages.brief: In parts of Mexico, a sinkhole has formed a lovely pool of cool, clean water, showing that sinkholes can be beautiful as well as destructive. The quiet pool sits in the landscape while, beneath the solid ground, water’s powerful effects on soil and rock continue.

books.art_why: Park rangers, parks, wildlife, and visitors are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Ever wonder what it’s like to be a park ranger? From preserving wilderness to teaching about historical events, park rangers are the backbone of our national and state parks. In Park Rangers, students will have an inside look at where rangers work, what they do, and what they need to know to get the job done.
pages.brief: A park ranger in uniform stands in a national park with mountains and trees behind, ready to lead visitors; the scene suggests a book about where rangers work, what they do, and how to become one.

pages.text: What’s It Like to Be a Park Ranger? Imagine being a park ranger. Picture yourself leading visitors to a beautiful hidden waterfall. Think about walking people step-by-step through an exciting battle from history. Imagine holding a turtle for schoolkids to touch. Imagine skiing into a snowy forest to save a hurt hiker.
pages.brief: In a set of imagined scenes, a park ranger leads visitors to a hidden waterfall, walks people through a historical battle, holds a turtle for schoolchildren to touch, and skis into a snowy forest to save a hurt hiker.

pages.text: Being a park ranger is a lot of work. Rangers work long hours. They work nights and weekends. They might hike for miles in a single day. They face wild animals and wild weather. Still, most rangers say it’s the best job in the world. Ranger Gear Rangers wear uniforms so visitors know who they are. They carry gear that helps them do their outdoor job. A typical ranger needs: • hiking boots • a sun hat • a radio • rope • a flashlight • a first-aid kit • sunscreen • bear spray* * Bear spray is high- powered pepper spray. If a wild animal attacks, bear spray can stop it.
pages.brief: A park ranger in uniform stands outdoors wearing hiking boots and a sun hat, with a radio, rope, flashlight, first-aid kit, sunscreen, and bear spray, ready for long hours, nights, weekends, miles of hiking, wild animals, and wild weather.

pages.text: Where Do Rangers Work? Park rangers work in national or state parks. Some parks are beautiful natural areas, such as the Grand Canyon and Yellowstone. Others are important places from history. Many parks include museums and public buildings. Some include memorials, which help us remember an event or a person who died.
pages.brief: Park rangers work in national and state parks, including the Grand Canyon and Yellowstone, and at historical places with museums, public buildings, and memorials; a ranger stands near a canyon, a memorial, and a museum.

pages.text: Parks are special places set aside for the future, but people visit parks today. They hike, ski, and fish in parks. They see beautiful art. They walk on beaches and rest near waterfalls. Park rangers work to keep all the visitors safe. Rangers also teach people about the park and how to save it for the future.
pages.brief: Visitors hike, ski, fish, look at beautiful art, walk on beaches, and rest near waterfalls in a special park, while a ranger watches over them and teaches people how to save the park for the future.

pages.text: What Do Rangers Do? Park rangers do many different jobs. Some rangers teach the public. At Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico, rangers teach people about bats while millions of them fly out of a cave. At George Washington’s birthplace in Virginia, rangers show how the Washington family ate dinner in the 1730s. At Alcatraz Island in California, rangers tell how some men escaped from the famous prison.
pages.brief: At Carlsbad Caverns, a ranger teaches visitors about bats flying out of a cave; at George Washington’s birthplace, a ranger shows a 1730s family dinner; at Alcatraz Island, a ranger tells how men escaped the famous prison.

pages.brief: In the Everglades, rangers work with scientists to track Florida panthers; in Banff, they monitor wildfires; at Navajo National Monument, they protect Native American ruins; on Cape Hatteras, they keep visitors from stepping on bird nests.

pages.text: Leader of the Pack Not everyone who works for the National Park Service is a ranger. Take biologist Doug Smith, who studies animals in Yellowstone National Park. “Everyone confuses biologists with rangers,” Smith says. In the early days of the Park Service, rangers did biology and everything else. Now, he says, “They're really involved with taking care of people.” Smith’s focus is more wolves than people. He came to Yellowstone in 1994 to help restore wolves to the park. Today, there are eleven packs in the park and 85–90 wolves. “In the park, it is clear that our mission is to restore natural systems, to bring nature back to the way it was before we messed it up,” Smith says. “So we did it, and we're doing it, and we're trying to understand it.”
pages.brief: Biologist Doug Smith stands in Yellowstone National Park observing wolves in the wild. He came in 1994 to help restore wolves, and today the park has eleven packs and 85–90 wolves living among the trees and hills.

pages.text: Other park rangers keep visitors safe. In the Great Smoky Mountains in Tennessee, rangers sign in every hiker. They make sure everyone comes home safely. If a hiker goes missing, rangers search the mountains. If a hiker is sick or hurt, rangers may need to fly the person out. Saving people can be dangerous. Rangers face flash floods, crumbling cliffs, and wild animals. In fact, park rangers have one of the riskiest jobs in the world!
pages.brief: In the Great Smoky Mountains, a ranger signs in hikers at a trailhead and searches the mountains for a missing hiker; another ranger helps fly out a sick or hurt person, facing flash floods, crumbling cliffs, and wild animals.

pages.text: What Do Rangers Need to Know? Rangers in different parks know about different things. At Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, a ranger shows visitors how lava created the mountains, caves, and sea cliffs. A history expert at the Statue of Liberty tells what the statue means to people moving to the United States. Musicians at the New Orleans Jazz Park play music the city is famous for.
pages.brief: At Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, a ranger shows visitors mountains, caves, and sea cliffs made by lava; at the Statue of Liberty, a history expert tells what the statue means to people moving to the United States; musicians play jazz in the New Orleans Jazz Park.

pages.text: Even rangers working in the same park are experts on different subjects. One ranger in Glacier National Park describes how glaciers shaped its beautiful valleys. An animal expert leads scientists to the park’s mountain goats. Another expert talks about the stars in the big, dark Montana sky. A ranger who knows first aid helps a hurt hiker.
pages.brief: In Glacier National Park, one ranger describes glacier-carved valleys, an animal expert leads scientists to mountain goats, another expert points out stars in the Montana sky, and a ranger with first aid helps a hurt hiker.

pages.text: Can I Be a Park Ranger? Does being a park ranger sound like fun? You can start by becoming a park volunteer. Volunteers do many of the same jobs as rangers. They learn about what goes on inside a park. Most rangers go to college. Some study history or science, while others study the wild lands and how people use them.
pages.brief: A park volunteer works alongside a ranger in a park, learning about what goes on inside a park; nearby, college students study history, science, wild lands, and how people use them to prepare for ranger jobs.

pages.text: Many people want to be park rangers. To get the job, you must show that you’re a hard worker and a good leader. If you love nature and history, and you want to help preserve it, you might make a great ranger! Parks in This Book CANADA 2 1 UNITED STATES 0 Hawaii MEXICO 1 8 2 9 3 0 4 a 5 b 6 c.
pages.brief: A hopeful future ranger stands in a park, showing hard work and good leadership, while a map shows parks across Canada, the United States, Hawaii, and Mexico for people who love nature and history and want to preserve it.

books.title: European Castles
books.art_why: Medieval castles predate photography, so the scenes must be drawn.

pages.text: What Is a Castle? During the Middle Ages, many castles were built across Europe. The castles were made to protect people from their enemies. They had thick, tall walls and watchtowers where guards stood watch over the castle. The people who owned the castles were the nobles. However, they were not the only people living in the castles. The people who served and protected the nobility also lived within the castle walls. The nobles not only owned and lived in the castle, they also owned much of the land stretching beyond the castle. They helped the monarch control the land.
pages.brief: A stone castle with thick tall walls and watchtowers stands in medieval Europe. Guards watch from the towers. Inside the walls, nobles and the people who serve and protect them live. Beyond the castle, the nobles’ land stretches out, land they help the monarch control.

pages.text: Living outside the castle was another class of people called commoners. They were the craftspeople and farmers who lived in small towns and villages and on farms not far from the castle. In exchange for living on the noble’s land, the commoners farmed the land and paid taxes to support the castle.
pages.brief: Outside the castle walls, commoners work as craftspeople and farmers in small towns, villages and farms. They live on the noble’s land. They farm the fields and pay taxes that help support the castle and its people.

pages.text: The First Castles The first type of castle was called a mott- and-bailey. The mott was a high mound of dirt with a wooden tower built upon it. A wooden fence, called a palisade, was built out from the mott. The palisade formed a wall surrounding the bailey, or the yard, that held the kitchen, hall, stables, and other buildings belonging to the noble.
pages.brief: A motte-and-bailey castle rises on a high mound of dirt. A wooden tower sits on top of the mound. A wooden palisade fence runs out from it and surrounds the bailey, the yard holding the kitchen, hall, stables and other buildings belonging to the noble.

pages.text: Later, castles had stone motts or towers. Many of these castles also featured moats. Moats were ditches, often filled with water, that surrounded the castle. As time passed, castles were built with bigger towers and walls. They became larger, with more rooms and passages. They came to look more and more like the large castles we see today. These castles were well built and have withstood the test of time.
pages.brief: A later stone castle has stone towers and a moat, a water-filled ditch surrounding it. Its towers and walls are bigger than earlier castles, with more rooms and passages. It looks like the large castles seen today and stands well built against time.

pages.text: Outside the Castle Newly built castles were painted with a mixture of lime and water. This mixture gave the castle walls a fresh, clean coat of white. For this reason, the mixture was called whitewash. Every castle’s design was different. Still, they had many of the same features. Most had towers or turrets, and many castles had an inner and an outer wall. Many also had a very strong building in the center of the castle. This building was called a keep.
pages.brief: A newly built castle is painted with whitewash, a lime and water mixture that gives its walls a fresh white coat. The castle has towers or turrets, an inner and outer wall, and a strong central building called the keep.

pages.text: Many castles were built in places that made them easier to defend. Many were built in the middle of lakes or on jagged hilltops and cliffs. This made it hard for attackers to reach the castle. The walls were often more than 3 meters (10 ft.) thick. The walls were topped with crenelations that gave them a sawtooth look. This design protected archers from enemy arrows. It also made it more difficult to climb over the walls. The primary entrance was through the main gate. But often there were smaller gates around the castle’s walls. These smaller gates were used for extra traffic or for deliveries to the kitchens.
pages.brief: A castle stands on a jagged hilltop or in a lake, making it hard for attackers to reach. Its walls are more than three meters thick and topped with sawtooth crenellations that protect archers. The main gate is the primary entrance, with smaller gates for extra traffic and kitchen deliveries.

pages.text: Castles had many windows to let light in. This meant that fewer candles and torches would be needed to light the rooms and halls. Windows near the ground were extremely narrow so that attackers could not climb through them. Since windows high above the ground were difficult to reach, they could be bigger. Most of these larger windows had shutters to keep out bad weather and often had bars to keep invaders out. The roofs and floors were made of hard wood. Many castles had cellars that were used to store food and wine. After the Middle Ages, dungeons were built in castle cellars. These dungeons were used to house prisoners.
pages.brief: A castle has many windows letting in light, so fewer candles and torches are needed. Narrow windows near the ground stop attackers from climbing in. Larger high windows have shutters and bars. Hard wood forms roofs and floors, and cellars store food and wine. Later cellars hold dungeons for prisoners.

pages.text: Inside the Castle Castles weren’t designed just to be defended. They were also designed to make life comfortable for the nobles. One of the most important places in a castle was the Great Hall. It was where meals, entertainment, and feasts were held. It was also where everyone gathered to talk or hold meetings. The kitchens were separated from the Great Hall by long passageways. Some kitchens were outside in another building to avoid the risk of the castles’ catching fire. This meant that food for could arrive at the tables cold or wet with rain!
pages.brief: Inside the castle, the Great Hall is where nobles and their household gather for meals, entertainment, feasts, talk and meetings. Long passageways separate the kitchens from the hall. Some kitchens stand in another building to avoid fire, so food can arrive cold or wet with rain.

pages.text: A castle had enough rooms to house the noble and their extended family. Visitors probably slept on straw mattresses in the Great Hall after the tables had been cleared away. Most castles had spiral staircases. They wound upward in a clockwise direction. They were built this way to slow down invaders by making it difficult to fight in the stairwells.
pages.brief: The castle has enough rooms for the noble and their extended family. After tables are cleared, visitors sleep on straw mattresses in the Great Hall. Spiral staircases wind upward clockwise, built to slow invaders and make fighting in the stairwell difficult.

pages.text: Built for Defense One of the most important things to consider in castle design was defense. A castle usually had two surrounding walls. The inner wall was taller than the outer one. Archers standing on the inner wall could fire their arrows over the defenders on the shorter wall. It also made it easier for those on the taller wall to defend against attackers who had reached the lower outer wall. The two sets of gates on these walls often opened at opposite ends of the castle. This forced invaders to circle around the inside of the outer wall to find the other gate. While looking for the second gate, invaders could be hit by the castle guards’ arrows.
pages.brief: A castle has two surrounding walls. The taller inner wall lets archers fire over defenders on the shorter outer wall and defend against attackers who reach it. The two gates open at opposite ends, forcing invaders to circle inside the outer wall while castle guards shoot arrows at them.

pages.text: Between the castle walls were the outer and inner wards. The outer ward was filled with shops and houses. The inner ward was where the food and weapons were stored, the knights stayed, and water wells were dug. In the center of the castle was a separate building called the keep. It was here that the nobility lived. It was the safest part of the castle and the hardest to enter. It was designed so that if the rest of the castle were captured, the nobles could still be defended.
pages.brief: Between the castle walls are the outer and inner wards. The outer ward holds shops and houses. The inner ward stores food and weapons, houses knights and has water wells. In the center, a separate keep is the safest building, where the nobility live and can still be defended if the rest of the castle is captured.

pages.text: People In and Around the Castle During the Middle Ages, life revolved around the church. People believed that God gave the kings and queens the power to rule. The church had at least as much power as the monarch. It represented the authority that gave the monarch the right to rule.
pages.brief: During the Middle Ages, life revolves around the church. People believe God gives kings and queens the power to rule. The church has at least as much power as the monarch and represents the authority that gives the monarch the right to rule.

pages.text: Under the king and queen were several other classes of people. The highest class was the nobles. They paid the monarch a tax for the privilege to control land in the kingdom. The knights also ranked high in the kingdom. Below the knights were the merchants and artisans. And below them were craftspeople and peasants, such as blacksmiths and farmers. All these people paid taxes to the nobles. Some of them were allowed to hold land.
pages.brief: Under the king and queen, nobles rank highest and pay the monarch a tax for the privilege to control land. Knights rank high below them. Then come merchants and artisans, then craftspeople and peasants such as blacksmiths and farmers. All pay taxes to nobles, and some are allowed to hold land.

pages.text: The lowest class was the peasants. They had to remain on the land where they were born. Peasants did not own land. These farmers had to give much of what they produced to the monarch and the landowner. A peasant’s life was tough. They paid high rents to the nobles and were hit worst during times of hunger, war, and illness. Many rebellions occurred due to the peasants’ unhappiness with the nobles, but these were almost always shut down by the ruling class.
pages.brief: The lowest class, peasants, must remain on the land where they were born. They do not own land and give much of what they produce to the monarch and landowner. Their life is tough, with high rents and hunger, war and illness. Rebellions against the nobles are almost always shut down by the ruling class.

pages.text: Castles and War Castles were the targets of many long- running wars. Sometimes, walls were built around entire towns. The peasants would defend this town wall for as long as they could. If the town wall were overrun, then knights would defend the outer wall of the castle. If that fell, then the inner wall was defended. And lastly, the center building, or keep, that housed the nobles was defended.
pages.brief: Castles are targets of long-running wars. Sometimes walls surround an entire town, and peasants defend the town wall as long as they can. If it is overrun, knights defend the castle’s outer wall, then the inner wall, and lastly the central keep that houses the nobles.

pages.text: Defending the castle was not easy. Enemies used many weapons to try to take over a castle. They used large battering rams to hammer away at the castle’s walls and gates. They used weapons called catapults to hurl rocks, debris, and even dead animals or people over the walls. Giant slingshot-like weapons called trebuchets were also used to hurl objects over the walls. And to discourage the castle defenders from rushing out of the castle to attack them, the attackers used giant crossbows mounted on carts.
pages.brief: Enemies attack the castle with large battering rams hammering the walls and gates. Catapults hurl rocks, debris and even dead animals or people over the walls. Giant slingshot-like trebuchets also throw objects. Giant crossbows mounted on carts discourage castle defenders from rushing out to attack.

pages.text: Many methods were used to keep attackers from entering a castle. Holes were cut into the floors of arches above the castle entrance. Defenders poured burning sand or tar on anyone trying to batter down the gates. Newer castles replaced arrow slits with keyhole-shaped windows where cannons could be placed.
pages.brief: Defenders cut holes into the floors of arches above the castle entrance. From these holes, they pour burning sand or tar on anyone trying to batter down the gates. Newer castles replace arrow slits with keyhole-shaped windows where cannons can be placed.

pages.text: The moat, often filled with water, surrounded the castle. It was difficult to tunnel under a moat, and attackers could not wade across the deep water. There is a myth that crocodiles were placed in some moats. Some moats did have eels and other kinds of fish in them for food, but there were no crocodiles.
pages.brief: A water-filled moat surrounds the castle. It is difficult to tunnel under the moat, and attackers cannot wade across its deep water. Some moats hold eels and other fish for food. A myth says crocodiles were placed in some moats, but there were no crocodiles.

pages.text: Often it was not possible to break into a well-built and well-defended castle. So the attackers would simply wait for the castle’s residents to run out of food or water.
pages.brief: A well-built and well-defended castle is often impossible to break into. Instead of attacking the walls, the attackers wait outside. They wait for the castle’s residents to run out of food or water.

pages.text: Around the 1600s, castles became less and less popular. They were no longer easy to defend because of the use of heavy cannons in warfare. The nobles also wanted more comfortable and open places to live. Still, many castles stand today as a reminder of an age gone by.
pages.brief: Around the 1600s, castles become less popular. Heavy cannons in warfare make them no longer easy to defend, and nobles want more comfortable, open places to live. Many castles still stand today as a reminder of an age gone by.

books.title: Fireworks
books.art_why: The book covers events over 1,000 years old and pre-photographic history, so drawings avoid fake photos.

pages.text: Fireworks is an informational book that details the history of fireworks. Techniques for making fireworks are included, as well as the planning required to create.
pages.brief: A bright fireworks display fills the night sky above a crowd, introducing a book about fireworks; varied bursts suggest the history of fireworks, how they are made, how a show is planned, and fireworks safety.

pages.text: Introduction The celebration began on a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean. Then, as Earth turned, midnight arrived in Sydney, Australia. Rings of fire exploded over the city’s famous opera house. Firecrackers popped in Hong Kong. Skyrockets flew over Bombay, the Egyptian pyramids, and Moscow. The Eiffel Tower shot bright sparks from its top like foam from a champagne bottle. Mexico City and Chicago were lit red, gold, and green. All around the world, fireworks welcomed the new year.
pages.brief: As midnight moves around the world, rings of fire burst over the Sydney Opera House, firecrackers pop in Hong Kong, and skyrockets fly over Bombay, the Egyptian pyramids, and Moscow. Bright sparks shoot from the Eiffel Tower, while Mexico City and Chicago glow red, gold, and green.

pages.text: Fireworks combine science and art to create some of the most beautiful displays ever seen. The making and launching of fireworks is called pyrotechnics (PIE-roe-TECK-nicks). In most cases, this dangerous craft is still performed by hand. Families pass down secret fireworks-making skills and formulas from generation to generation.
pages.brief: A fireworks maker works by hand, carefully combining materials for a display. An older family member shows a younger one secret fireworks-making skills and formulas, passing the dangerous craft from generation to generation, while colorful fireworks glow in the night sky.

pages.text: History of Fireworks No one is sure when fireworks first shot into the sky. But we do know that it happened in China over 1,000 years ago. Legend says that a Chinese cook accidentally created gunpowder by mixing ingredients in his kitchen.
pages.brief: In a Chinese kitchen long ago, a cook accidentally mixes ingredients and creates gunpowder. He looks surprised as the explosive black powder forms, while outside the sky is dark and calm, far from the fireworks that would later shoot into the sky.

pages.text: Chinese people packed this explosive black powder into bamboo or paper tubes. The powder shot fire out of the tubes, much like Roman candles do today. Someone discovered that if a wooden carving was placed on top of the gunpowder, the carving would shoot into the sky. One carving of a dragon even had gunpowder in its mouth. The dragon seemed to spray fire as it flew.
pages.brief: Chinese people pack explosive black powder into bamboo and paper tubes. Fire shoots from the tubes like Roman candles. A wooden dragon carving with gunpowder in its mouth is placed on top, then flies into the sky, seeming to spray fire as it goes.

pages.text: The secret of gunpowder passed to countries in the Middle East and then on to Europe. But it was mostly used in weapons to fire cannons and guns. Often, armies shot their cannons to celebrate a victory. Different countries began mixing certain chemicals with the gunpowder to create brighter flashes, louder bangs, and color. The Italians soon became famous for their colorful displays. The Grucci family, now living in the United States, continues the Italian tradition of fireworks mastery.
pages.brief: The secret of gunpowder travels to the Middle East and Europe, where armies fire cannons and guns. Cannons boom in celebration after a victory. Fireworks makers in different countries add chemicals for brighter flashes, louder bangs, and color; Italian displays become famous, and the Grucci family carries the tradition to the United States.

pages.text: How Fireworks Are Made All fireworks start with gunpowder. To create colors, fireworks makers combine special chemicals with the gunpowder. These chemicals burn with different-colored flames. Surprisingly, most of these chemicals are kinds of salt. They may also mix flakes of metal with the gunpowder. When the powder explodes, these flakes become glowing hot, creating a shower of sparks.
pages.brief: A fireworks maker combines special chemicals and flakes of metal with gunpowder. The chemicals burn with colored flames, while the metal flakes become glowing hot when the powder explodes, creating a shower of sparks. Small piles of ingredients and a burst of sparks show how every firework starts with gunpowder.

pages.text: Different chemicals burn with different colors. Copper, the metal in pennies, burns blue-green. The same color change happens, only much more slowly, to pennies when they turn green. This is why the Statue of Liberty, which is made of copper, looks green. The chart below lists some other chemicals and the colors they produce. Fireworks Chemicals Chemical Effect Copper salts Blue Strontium salts Red Sodium Yellow Barium nitrate Green Potassium perchlorate Makes loud booms.
pages.brief: Samples of copper salts, strontium salts, sodium, barium nitrate, and potassium perchlorate burn in different colors: blue-green, red, yellow, green, and loud booms. The green Statue of Liberty stands nearby, reminding viewers that copper slowly turns green, the same color change as copper burns.

pages.text: Fireworks cause sound because the intense heat expands the air around the firework. The air is pushed outward in a wave. Your ear picks up this wave as a loud sound. Sometimes your chest and feet can also feel the wave vibrating. This is the same way that lightning creates thunder. The whistles come from the hot gasses combustion creates. Fireworks makers put tiny paper whistles inside the shells. When the stars combust, the hot gasses “blow” the whistles, creating the sound.
pages.brief: A firework bursts high above, and a person nearby feels the loud sound wave in their chest and feet. A lightning bolt and thundercloud show the same effect. Inside a shell, hot gases from combustion blow tiny paper whistles, creating the whistling sound.

pages.text: Fireworks makers roll the colored or sparkling gunpowder into small balls called stars. Some stars are a single color, while others are layered with different colors. They pack the stars inside stiff paper shells. Hundreds of stars can fit in one shell. If the fireworks maker packs the stars in a globe shape, the firework will explode in a globe of fire. If he or she packs it in a star shape, it will explode into a star. If he or she packs it in a smiley-face shape, it will explode into a smiley face. Parts of a Firework.
pages.brief: A fireworks maker rolls colored or sparkling gunpowder into small balls called stars, some single-colored and some layered. The stars are packed inside stiff paper shells. A globe-shaped shell, a star-shaped shell, and a smiley-face-shaped shell show how packing the stars shapes the explosion.

pages.text: Sometimes each star has its own paper tube. The tubes force the stars to shoot away from the main firework in streaks of light. And sometimes the shell is packed solid with powder that creates a single flash and a huge bang, called a salute. At the center of every shape is a ball of gunpowder called a bursting charge. The bursting charge explodes like a firecracker. It lights the stars and sends them out into the sky.
pages.brief: Some stars sit in their own paper tubes, forcing them to shoot away in streaks of light. A salute shell is packed solid with powder for a single flash and a huge bang. At the center, a bursting charge explodes like a firecracker and sends the lit stars into the sky.

pages.text: 1 The last part of the shell is the lift charge. This is a container of powder that will shoot the entire shell high into the sky. Usually, the lift charge is ordinary gunpowder. But sometimes it creates a streak of color as the firework rises.
pages.brief: A cutaway illustration shows the last part of a firework shell: the lift charge, a container of powder that shoots the entire shell high into the sky. Usually ordinary gunpowder, the lift charge sometimes creates a colored streak as the firework rises.

pages.text: Do You Know? Combustion is the scientific term for burning or exploding. Almost all combustion requires oxygen. A flame under a glass dome will soon go out when it uses up all the oxygen. Gunpowder has oxygen right in it, which makes it extra flammable. Combustion also makes the air around it expand, or grow larger. When gunpowder combusts inside a shell, the air inside the shell expands, forcing the shell to burst open.
pages.brief: A flame under a glass dome dims as it uses up oxygen. A shell is shown bursting as gunpowder combusts inside; the air around it expands and forces the shell open. Combustion, the scientific term for burning or exploding, needs oxygen, and gunpowder carries oxygen within it.

pages.text: Each firework has a special series of fuses that control when the firework explodes. The first fuse, called a leader, lights the lift charge, sending the firework flying. The lift charge then lights a time fuse. The material of the time fuse burns at a steady rate. The fireworks makers know just how long to cut the fuse so it burns until the shell is at the right height. The time fuse then sets off the bursting charge. Sometimes a shell will have smaller shells inside it. In that case, the bursting charge lights more time fuses. These will set off the smaller away from the main shell.
pages.brief: A series of fuses controls the firework. A leader lights the lift charge and sends the shell flying. Then a time fuse burns at a steady rate until the shell reaches the right height. The time fuse sets off the bursting charge, which can light smaller shells and send them away from the main shell.

pages.text: Creating the Show It can take up to two days to set up a twenty-minute fireworks show. First, everything must be designed on a diagram. Each shell will be fired in a specific order, must be set up so that each one goes in turn. Workers begin by building batteries, or wooden racks. If the show is near water, the batteries are put on a boat, safely away from the crowd. Some batteries sit on the sides of buildings, such as the Washington Monument or the Eiffel Tower. Each battery holds a group of metal tubes called mortars. Each mortar holds one shell. It shoots the shell the way a cannon shoots a cannonball. All the mortars are numbered according to the diagram.
pages.brief: Workers build wooden racks called batteries and fill metal tubes called mortars with shells. Near water, the batteries sit on a boat; elsewhere they stand beside buildings such as the Washington Monument or the Eiffel Tower. A diagram guides the order, so every shell fires in turn.

pages.text: The finished shells are also numbered. When they arrive on the site, they are carefully placed in the correct mortars. Workers connect the shells’ leaders, or main fuses, to electrical matches. And each electric match is connected to the firing panel, which is the control panel for the whole show. In the past, the fireworks maker had to push buttons on the panel to get each match to light. He or she had to pay close attention in order to avoid mistakes. Today, most firing panels are computerized.
pages.brief: Finished shells are carefully placed in the correct mortars. Workers connect the shells' leaders to electrical matches, and each match connects to a firing panel. In the past, a fireworks maker pushed buttons on the panel; today, most firing panels are computerized and control the show.

pages.text: Everyone checks the fuse connections, the placement of the shells and mortars, and the firing order. Then they check them again. A mistake could set the fireworks off incorrectly, ruining the show and possibly even injuring people.
pages.brief: Everyone checks the fuse connections, the placement of shells and mortars, and the firing order. Then they check everything again. A mistake could set the fireworks off incorrectly, ruining the show and possibly injuring people, so the crew examines each connection with care.

pages.text: On the night of the show, the crew puts on helmets, goggles, and fireproof clothing. This gear protects the workers from falling sparks, ash, and paper. The workers stay close by to make sure nothing goes wrong. But once the switch is flipped, the computer takes over and begins lighting matches. The show explodes in a shower of color and sound.
pages.brief: On the night of the show, the crew wears helmets, goggles, and fireproof clothing to protect against falling sparks, ash, and paper. They stay close by as a switch is flipped. The computer takes over, lighting matches, and the show explodes in a shower of color and sound.

pages.text: Computer firing panels have become so precise that fireworks can be set to music. A designer chooses a favorite piece of music. The designer listens to the music over and over, imagining where to put a purple fountain, a golden blast, or flashes and crashes. The firing panel is programmed to light the shells in time with the music.
pages.brief: A designer chooses a favorite piece of music and listens to it over and over, imagining where to place a purple fountain, a golden blast, or flashes and crashes. The computerized firing panel is programmed to light the shells in time with the music.

pages.text: Fireworks Safety Fireworks explode, and explosions can be deadly. Fireworks injure about 10,000 people every year in the United States alone. Firecrackers can blow off a hand. Sparklers can send a glowing-hot spark of metal into someone’s eye. And illegally stored fireworks can cause devastating fires. In addition, fireworks cause smoke and noise, and they often terrify animals and alarm people. Many states have laws against using fireworks. Those laws exist to protect people. Using, storing, or selling illegal fireworks can lead to arrest, fines, or even jail. It is best to leave fireworks to the trained professionals.
pages.brief: Fireworks explode, and explosions can be deadly. A firecracker can blow off a hand, and a sparkler can send glowing-hot metal into an eye. Illegally stored fireworks can cause devastating fires; smoke and noise terrify animals and alarm people. Laws against fireworks exist to protect people, so leave fireworks to trained professionals.

pages.text: If you do watch fireworks, be sure to follow these safety tips: • Always watch from a safe distance, and never approach the fireworks. • Never pick up debris from fireworks. It may still contain explosive gunpowder. • Bring ear protection. Long exposure to loud noises can damage your hearing. • Never, ever light fireworks yourself. If consumer fireworks are legal in your state, always have an adult light them. • Have water handy to put out any fires or sparks.
pages.brief: A person watches fireworks from a safe distance and never approaches them. They wear ear protection, keep water handy for fires or sparks, and leave all debris alone because it may still contain explosive gunpowder. An adult lights consumer fireworks only where they are legal.

books.title: Amelia Earhart: A Legend in Flight
books.art_why: The book is about a named famous person, Amelia Earhart.

pages.text: A Legend in Flight Amelia Earhart: A Legend in Flight provides students with a historical look at Earhart’s life. Students will enjoy this text about a woman who has become both a hero and role model for her accomplishments in flying. Photographs and maps accompany the text.
pages.brief: Amelia Earhart, a woman pilot, stands near an early airplane. A vintage map and a few photographs of her life are arranged nearby, suggesting a historical look at her accomplishments in flying. The scene introduces her story.

pages.text: Introduction The airplane bounced among the clouds. Giant black storm clouds lay ahead. The year was 1932. The airplane carried Amelia Earhart. She had been the first woman to ride in an airplane over the Atlantic Ocean. Now, if she made it, she would be the first woman to fly an airplane over the Atlantic. And she would be the first person to have crossed the Atlantic in an airplane twice. But first she had to succeed, and the trip was dangerous. Airplanes in the 1930s were small, and they didn’t have the instruments that today’s pilots do. A pilot had to go by her sense of sight, keeping tight control of the airplane.
pages.brief: A small 1930s airplane carrying Amelia Earhart bounces among clouds, with giant black storm clouds looming ahead. Inside, Amelia peers through the cockpit, using sight to keep tight control because the plane has few instruments.

pages.text: The black clouds ahead were too large to fly around, so Amelia pointed the little plane right into them. Ice froze the plane’s controls, sending it into a tailspin. Amelia struggled to get control. Finally, the ice melted and Amelia was able to pull the plane out of its spin. Many hours later, Amelia set the plane down in Northern Ireland. She had crossed the Atlantic Ocean in an airplane she flew herself. She had already been famous. Now, she would be a legend. But Amelia Earhart would be most remembered for something else. While trying to fly around the world, she disappeared.
pages.brief: Amelia points her small airplane straight into huge black clouds. Ice forms on the controls and the plane spins in a tailspin; Amelia grips the controls and struggles. Later, she sets the plane down in Northern Ireland, having flown across the Atlantic herself.

pages.text: Winged Machines The world’s first airplane flight happened in 1903. Two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, successfully flew their winged machine in North Carolina. Many people thought the idea of flying was exciting. It was also dangerous. Planes were fragile and slow. They did not fly well in bad weather, and many pilots died in crashes. By 1937, airplanes had improved a lot. Engineers designed better airplanes, but accidents still happened.
pages.brief: Wilbur and Orville Wright stand beside their fragile winged machine on a sandy field in North Carolina in 1903. The early airplane looks slow and delicate. Nearby, other early planes and pilots show how dangerous flying was before engineers improved airplanes by 1937.

pages.text: Kansas Youth Anyone who knew Amelia as a child could hardly have been surprised by her later accomplishments. She was born in Kansas in 1897. She spent most of her time with her family and friends. They climbed around the banks of the Missouri River. Amelia made up games for the children to play. She and her sister were such active children that their mother made “ bloomers ” for them to wear. Unlike dresses, bloomers allowed the girls to be as active as the boys. When Amelia was twenty-one, her family moved to California. One day she attended an air show. The airplanes dazzled her, flying in loops and doing stunts. She knew then that she wanted to fly. With her parents’ help, Amelia took piloting lessons and saved enough money to buy an airplane. Before long, she was flying in air shows herself.
pages.brief: Young Amelia Earhart climbs along the banks of the Missouri River with her sister and friends in Kansas. She wears bloomers made by her mother so she can run and play. Later, as a young woman in California, she watches airplanes loop and stunt at an air show, dazzled.

pages.text: Time to Fly Amelia later moved to Boston and found a job at Denison House. It was a place where people who were poor, especially children, could receive help. She loved her work there, but then the chance of a lifetime presented itself. George Putnam, a publicist, searched for a woman to be the first to ride in an airplane over the Atlantic. It was a dangerous idea. Three women had died trying to cross the Atlantic the year before.
pages.brief: Amelia Earhart works at Denison House in Boston, helping poor families and children. In a busy room, she sits with children and adults who need assistance. Elsewhere, publicist George Putnam searches for a woman brave enough to ride in an airplane across the Atlantic.

pages.text: Only men had ever crossed the Atlantic in an airplane. Anyone who would try it had to withstand danger and fatigue. George thought Amelia Earhart was perfect, and she was eager to go. Amelia Earhart: Flier and...? In her lifetime, Amelia worked at many jobs. At that time, it was unusual for women to have jobs at all! • Nurse • Magazine editor • Social worker • Writer • Pilot • Airline executive • Clothing designer • Professor She also helped start the “Ninety-Nines,” a group of women pilots that still exists today.
pages.brief: Amelia Earhart is shown in a series of scenes: as a nurse, magazine editor, social worker, writer, pilot, airline executive, clothing designer and professor. A group of women pilots stands together, representing the Ninety-Nines she helped start.

pages.text: Amelia was just a passenger on that 1928 flight, but her life would never be the same. The first woman to cross the Atlantic made headlines around the world. After the flight, she was famous and busy writing books and giving speeches about flying. She also designed clothing and luggage for active women like herself and even helped launch two airlines. Later, she married George Putnam. She also continued to fly.
pages.brief: Amelia Earhart steps from an airplane after her 1928 flight across the Atlantic, greeted by crowds and newspaper photographers. Later, she writes books, gives speeches, designs clothing and luggage for active women, helps launch airlines, marries George Putnam, and keeps flying.

pages.text: By the time she was thirty-nine years old, Amelia had made every major flight there was, except for one. The greatest challenge left was to fly around the world. Only one pilot had ever flown around the world. But he didn’t follow the equator, the longest and most difficult route. This was the route Amelia would fly. Would she make it? By this time, no one doubted Amelia Earhart’s flying skill. On May 21, 1937, she took off with her navigator, Fred Noonan. They went to Florida in Electra.
pages.brief: Amelia Earhart, thirty-nine, stands with her navigator Fred Noonan beside the Electra airplane. On May 21, 1937, they prepare to take off on a daring flight around the world along the equator, the longest and most difficult route.

pages.text: ASIA ASIA AFRICA AFRICA SOUTH SOUTH AMERICA AMERICA Last Flight Amelia and Fred first stopped the Electra in Florida. The new plane had crossed the entire North American continent. Next, they flew to South America, Africa, India, Asia, and Australia. It appeared that Amelia Earhart would once again pull off a historic flight without a hitch. On June 29, 1937, they stopped in New Guinea, just north of Australia. There, they fueled the airplane and checked their maps. When they took off again, there was no hint of any trouble to come.
pages.brief: A world map traces the Electra's route from Florida across South America, Africa, India, Asia, and Australia. Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan stop in New Guinea, north of Australia, where they fuel the airplane and check their maps before taking off again.

pages.text: ASIA ASIA India India Hawaii Howland Island Lae AUSTRALIA AUSTRALIA As they flew close to Howland Island, their radio messages became odd. The U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca waited offshore to receive their signals and help them find the island. Those radio signals were irregular and strange. Amelia spoke of a storm, yet the weather over the island was clear. More than twenty hours into the flight, Amelia’s voice said, “We’re running north and south.” She was never heard from again.
pages.brief: Amelia Earhart's airplane flies near Howland Island while the U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca waits offshore. Radio signals are irregular and strange. Amelia speaks of a storm even though the sky over the island is clear; more than twenty hours into the flight, her voice is heard for the last time.

pages.text: What Happened to Amelia? This question is still a mystery today. The Itasca and the U.S. Navy began searching for Amelia’s plane. The search continued for weeks.
