No sign of the plane, Amelia, or Fred was found. After a year of searching, Amelia’s husband believed that she died at sea. But is that the full story? Some people think Amelia and Fred survived an emergency landing and were picked up by a Japanese ship.
pages.brief: The U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca and U.S. Navy ships search the wide ocean for Amelia's missing plane. Weeks pass with no sign of Amelia, Fred, or the Electra. Amelia's husband believes she died at sea, while others imagine an emergency landing and rescue by a Japanese ship.

pages.text: Others think that Amelia landed the plane, but at a different island. There, she and Fred were able to live on native foods but died of either sickness or old age. Many people believe the easiest answer is that the plane landed in the water. Perhaps Amelia and Fred drowned before they inflated their life raft. Whatever happened, there is no doubt that Amelia Earhart is one of the greatest Americans of the 20th century. She showed everyone that women didn’t have to live with limits. She showed people that anyone could fly. She was a legend.
pages.brief: Some people picture Amelia and Fred landing on a different island and surviving on native foods until sickness or old age. Others imagine the plane landing in the water, with Amelia and Fred drowning before inflating their life raft. A final portrait shows Amelia as a legendary pilot who proved women had no limits.

books.title: Queen Elizabeth I
books.art_why: A named famous historical person with no photographs from her lifetime.

pages.text: Queen Elizabeth l.
pages.brief: A formal portrait of Queen Elizabeth I, the English queen, shown alone against a simple royal background. She looks directly at the viewer with a calm, commanding expression, her posture upright and regal, representing the famous ruler named in the book.

pages.text: Elizabeth’s Family Many people think Elizabeth Tudor was the greatest English ruler of all time. She came from a powerful family. Before Elizabeth was born, her father, King Henry VIII of England, fell in love with Anne Boleyn while he was still married to his first wife. Henry wanted to end his marriage and marry Anne. This was not allowed in the Catholic Church at the time. Against the wishes of the Catholic Church, Henry started another church and ended his marriage. This church became known as the Church of England.
pages.brief: King Henry VIII of England stands with Anne Boleyn in a royal court, while his first wife is shown apart. Henry looks determined as he turns away from the Catholic Church and begins the Church of England, with church leaders and courtiers nearby.

pages.text: Henry was free of the Catholic Church. He married Anne Boleyn. Anne gave birth to Elizabeth Tudor on September 7, 1533. Anne was worried after she gave birth to Elizabeth. She thought that Henry might be unhappy with her for not giving him a son. She was right. Henry already had a daughter, Mary, with his first wife. He wanted a son to take over as king when he died. In time, Henry ended their marriage and had her put to death. Elizabeth was only three years old when her mother died.
pages.brief: Anne Boleyn lies in a royal bed after giving birth to baby Elizabeth Tudor, looking worried. King Henry VIII stands sternly nearby, and in the background young Mary is shown. A somber scene suggests Anne’s marriage ending and her death while Elizabeth is three.

pages.text: Prince Edward In 1537, Henry married his third wife, Jane, who gave birth to Prince Edward. At last, Henry had the son he always wanted. Jane, however, died a few days after Edward was born. Henry’s sixth and last wife was Catherine Parr. She told Henry to decide who would one day take over his throne, and finally he did. Prince Edward would be first in line, Mary would be second, and Elizabeth would be third. When Henry VIII died in 1547, nine-year-old Prince Edward became king. His rule as king was short. Edward died when he was only fifteen years old. Elizabeth’s older sister Mary became queen.
pages.brief: King Henry VIII stands with Jane and baby Prince Edward; Jane looks weak after childbirth. Catherine Parr speaks with Henry about the throne. Young Edward is later shown crowned king, then a solemn scene shows Edward gone and Mary becoming queen.

pages.text: Mary and Elizabeth Mary had been raised in the Catholic religion. In her time, some people began a new Protestant religion. Mary’s goal as queen was to end the Protestant religion and make the Catholic religion England’s main religion again. Mary did not like people who did not follow the Catholic teachings. She was known for her strict punishments and often ordered Protestants to be put to death. This earned her the nickname “Bloody Mary.” Elizabeth, on the other hand, was Protestant. The faith was important to her, but Elizabeth attended Catholic church to please Mary. Mary didn’t trust Elizabeth and believed she was practicing the Protestant faith in secret. When some people plotted to remove Mary as queen, she was sure that Elizabeth was behind it. Mary had Elizabeth arrested and put in jail for two months. When Elizabeth was let go, she remained under Mary’s watch for a year.
pages.brief: Queen Mary, wearing Catholic royal robes, looks stern as Protestants are punished. Elizabeth attends a Catholic church while secretly holding Protestant faith. Mary watches Elizabeth with suspicion, then has her arrested and confined in a jail cell for two months, with guards keeping watch afterward.

pages.text: Queen Elizabeth In 1558, Mary became ill and died. Elizabeth, who was next in line to the throne, was crowned queen on January 15, 1559. Elizabeth announced to the world that she was a Protestant. However, Elizabeth had an open mind. She worked with both Catholics and Protestants and tried to make peace. She was not always successful. Protestants thought she was too easy on Catholics, and some Catholics felt she turned her back on them.
pages.brief: Elizabeth is crowned queen in a grand royal ceremony on January 15, 1559, wearing a crown and royal robes. She stands before Catholic and Protestant leaders with an open, thoughtful expression, while groups on both sides look uncertain, showing her attempt to make peace between them.

pages.text: From the beginning of Elizabeth’s time as queen, English leaders tried to find a husband for her. If Elizabeth married and had a child, England would have a future king or queen. Elizabeth received many offers to marry but did not accept any. Elizabeth’s Fashion Elizabeth had fair skin and hair, features considered beautiful in Tudor England. As a young girl, Elizabeth dressed modestly, but as queen, she preferred to wear gowns of bright reds and oranges. Her robes were often decorated with rich pearls and jewels. Such elaborate clothing gave a sense of absolute royal power and authority.
pages.brief: English leaders present suitors and marriage offers to Queen Elizabeth, but she turns away calmly. In a royal dressing scene, Elizabeth wears a bright red and orange gown decorated with pearls and jewels. Her fair skin and hair are shown, and her elaborate clothing conveys royal power and authority.

pages.text: Battles Elizabeth faced many challenges, but one of her biggest problems came from Mary, Queen of Scots. Mary, Elizabeth’s cousin, was the Catholic queen of Scotland. Many Catholics didn’t think Elizabeth should be queen. Different Catholic groups plotted to remove Elizabeth so Mary could be the English queen. They wanted England to be a Catholic country. In 1586, Elizabeth learned that there was a plot to kill her. Mary was involved. Elizabeth had her put to death. Mary died on February 8, 1587. Her death angered Catholics everywhere. King Philip II of Spain, a Catholic, was one of them. Philip thought that Queen Elizabeth had gone too far and should be removed as queen. He also wanted England to be a Catholic country again.
pages.brief: Mary, Queen of Scots, a Catholic queen, stands with plotting nobles who want Elizabeth removed. Elizabeth learns of a plot to kill her and orders Mary’s death. Across Europe, King Philip II of Spain reacts with anger, determined to remove Elizabeth and return England to the Catholic faith.

pages.text: In 1588, Philip ordered a large group of ships to set sail and invade England. The ships were loaded with soldiers. Spain, however, was not prepared for the strength of the English. English ships forced the Spanish ships far to the north. Many Spanish ships crashed on the rocky shores, and many men died. Route of the Spanish, 1588.
pages.brief: King Philip II of Spain sends a large group of ships loaded with soldiers to invade England in 1588. English ships force the Spanish fleet far north, and many Spanish ships crash on rocky shores. The scene shows the dangerous sea route and the disaster for Spain.

pages.text: Elizabeth’s Successes Over time, Elizabeth reduced the religious fighting that had torn apart her country. The Protestant church became the official religion of England. There was great growth in education and the arts. More people than ever before learned to read and write. Theater became very popular during Elizabeth’s time and writers often brought plays and actors to her court. Some plays were about the events happening in England at the time, and some were comedies that Elizabeth enjoyed. She also loved poetry and playing music.
pages.brief: Queen Elizabeth sits in her court as writers bring plays and actors before her. Nearby, adults and children read and write, showing growth in education. The theater is busy and popular, and Elizabeth enjoys a comedy, poetry, and music in a lively, cultured royal setting.

pages.text: During her time as queen, Elizabeth developed a strong government and a powerful navy. Wanting to bring good things to the country she loved, she encouraged exploration of new places and trade with foreign countries. Trade of goods such as silk and food made money for England. England was set to become a global empire and the Elizabethan Age came to be known as the “Golden Age” in English history. As a result of growth during this time, England became one of the most important countries in the world.
pages.brief: Queen Elizabeth stands with government advisers and naval officers beside a busy harbor. English ships return with silk and food from foreign trade, and explorers set out for new places. The prosperous scene shows England growing into a powerful global empire during the Elizabethan Age.

pages.text: A Strong Leader Elizabeth died in 1603 at the age of sixty- nine. She ruled England for forty-four years. She named Protestant James VI, the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, as the new king. By doing so, she united Scotland and England. Elizabeth I was a well-educated, strong queen. She proved that a woman could be a successful ruler. At the same time, she earned the love and respect of her people.
pages.brief: An older Queen Elizabeth lies peacefully at the end of her reign in 1603, with a crown nearby. James VI of Scotland is shown as the new king, joining Scotland and England. Around Elizabeth, her people look on with love and respect for their strong, well-educated queen.

pages.text: Queen Elizabeth I 1533: Elizabeth born to Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn 1536: Anne Boleyn executed 1544: Henry orders his son and daughters as future leaders 1547: Henry VIII dies; Edward becomes king 1553: King Edward VI dies on July 6 1553: Mary crowned queen on October 1 1554: Mary orders Elizabeth jailed 1558: Mary dies; Elizabeth becomes queen 1587: Mary, Queen of Scots dies 1588: Elizabeth wins the fight against the Spanish 1603: Elizabeth dies on March 24; James I becomes king of England and Scotland, bringing the two countries together 1590: The arts begin to grow due to the support of Elizabeth.
pages.brief: A grand portrait of Queen Elizabeth I stands at the center of a sequence of small scenes from her life: her birth, Anne Boleyn’s execution, Henry VIII’s death, Edward as king, Mary as queen, Elizabeth jailed, Elizabeth crowned, Mary Queen of Scots’ death, the Spanish defeat, Elizabeth’s death, James I uniting the countries, and the arts growing.

books.title: Jackie Robinson
books.art_why: The book is a biography of a named famous person, Jackie Robinson.

pages.text: Baseball is known as America’s pastime, and many people enjoy playing and watching this sport. But, did you know there was a time when black athletes were not allowed to play on the same teams as white athletes? Jackie Robinson tells the story of the man who changed that. Detailed photographs and engaging text will keep students interested in this important part of American history.
pages.brief: A baseball scene showing players and spectators enjoying America’s pastime, with a portrait of Jackie Robinson set beside it. The image introduces the story of the man who helped change the time when black athletes could not play on the same teams as white athletes.

pages.text: Introduction African Americans play a big part in professional sports today. For many years, however, black athletes weren’t allowed to play with white athletes. Jackie Robinson helped change all that.
pages.brief: A modern professional sports stadium filled with diverse athletes and cheering fans, showing African American players competing alongside white players on the same field. In the foreground, a thoughtful image of Jackie Robinson in a baseball cap looks toward the field, recalling the change he helped bring about.

pages.text: The Early Years Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born into a poor Georgia family in 1919.
pages.brief: A poor Georgia family in 1919 gathers in a simple wooden home around a baby boy, Jack Roosevelt Robinson, wrapped in a blanket. The room is plain and modest, with few belongings, showing the family’s hard circumstances.

pages.text: In college, he was a star on his school’s football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. His family had little money, however. He left college in 1941 to help support his family. He did not finish college.
pages.brief: A young Jackie Robinson in a college sports uniform stands on a field surrounded by football, track, basketball, and baseball equipment, smiling as teammates practice behind him. A small, worn dormitory nearby suggests his family had little money and he left school to help support them.

pages.text: Taking a Stand In December 1941, the United States entered a war. Like many young men, Robinson had to serve in the war. One day, he and a group of soldiers got on an army bus. The bus was segregated. White soldiers sat in the front and black soldiers in the back. Yet Robinson knew he was as good a soldier as the white men. He would not move to the back when he was told to. Robinson was arrested, but he had only stood up for what was right. He was let go.
pages.brief: Inside a segregated army bus, Jackie Robinson stands firm in the aisle while a group of soldiers looks on. White soldiers sit at the front and black soldiers at the back. Robinson refuses to move to the back, his expression determined, as military police approach to arrest him.

pages.text: You’re Hired! After his time in the army, Robinson played baseball. In 1945, however, baseball was segregated, too. White and black athletes played in different leagues.
pages.brief: A 1945 baseball field split into two separate leagues, with white players in one dugout and black players in another, both groups playing the same game but kept apart. Jackie Robinson stands at the edge, holding a bat and watching the divided teams, his face serious.

pages.text: Robinson felt that there should not be different baseball leagues based on skin color. So did Branch Rickey. He ran the Brooklyn Dodgers. Rickey wanted the Dodgers to be the first white team with a black player. Rickey knew that this player would not only have to be great at baseball. He would also have to face prejudice because he was African American.
pages.brief: Branch Rickey, a serious older man in a suit, stands in the Brooklyn Dodgers office with Jackie Robinson. Rickey gestures toward a Dodgers cap and a baseball roster, explaining that Robinson would be the first black player on a white team and would have to face prejudice.

pages.text: Rickey hired Robinson. He had one condition, though. Robinson could only fight prejudice one way—by playing great baseball. A Team of Two A Team of Two.
pages.brief: Branch Rickey shakes hands with Jackie Robinson across a desk, a Brooklyn Dodgers cap between them. Rickey holds up one finger, showing the single condition: Robinson can fight prejudice only by playing great baseball. Robinson nods, determined, in a quiet office.

pages.text: Number 42 Takes the Field Wearing number 42, Robinson took the field on April 15, 1947. A crowd of twenty-six thousand people watched as he walked to the plate. Insults rang out from the other team’s dugout. Robinson just played ball.
pages.brief: On April 15, 1947, Jackie Robinson, wearing number 42 on his Brooklyn Dodgers uniform, walks to the plate before a crowd of twenty-six thousand spectators. Players in the opposing dugout lean out and shout insults, but Robinson keeps his eyes on the pitcher and simply plays ball.

pages.text: Equal rights won that day. So did the Dodgers. As for Robinson, he went on to have a great career. Another Great Steal Another Great Steal.
pages.brief: A triumphant baseball scene: Jackie Robinson rounds the bases in his Dodgers uniform while teammates celebrate and a large crowd cheers. The joyful team and fans show equal rights winning that day and the Dodgers winning too, as Robinson goes on to a great career.

pages.text: In 1962, he became the first African American to get into the Baseball Hall of Fame.
pages.brief: In 1962, Jackie Robinson stands in the Baseball Hall of Fame, holding a plaque and smiling. Around him are displays of baseball memorabilia and a crowd of admirers; he is shown as the first African American inducted into the Hall of Fame.

pages.text: His Number, His Day His Number, His Day.
pages.brief: A baseball stadium celebration honoring Jackie Robinson, with his Dodgers uniform and the number 42 displayed prominently while players and fans gather. The scene shows that his number and a special day are remembered, with respectful, joyful faces in the crowd.

pages.text: Beyond Baseball Robinson stopped playing baseball in 1957. Then he went into business. He also continued to work for equal rights for all people. He died in 1972. Today in the United States, more people of color play in the world of sports than ever before. We all have Number 42 to thank for that.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson in a business suit stands in an office, then beside a diverse group of people advocating equal rights. In the background, today’s sports field is filled with players of color, showing his lasting impact after he stopped playing baseball in 1957.

books.title: Slithery Snakes
books.art_why: Real snakes and their natural habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: Snakes are among the animal kingdom’s most amazing predators. Their ability to adapt to the natural world has enabled them to survive on every continent except Antarctica. Slithery Snakes provides students with a comprehensive look at these fascinating creatures that play an important role in Earth’s natural environment.
pages.brief: A wide view of several snakes in natural habitats on different continents around the world shows these amazing predators surviving in the wild; no snakes are shown in a clear, cold, snowy, faraway Antarctic setting.

pages.text: Introduction Snakes are reptiles, a class of animals that also includes lizards and turtles. Snakes have no limbs. They come in many lengths, patterns, and colors. There are several thousand types of snakes. They live in oceans, in trees, and on land, and they have adapted to survive in unusual ways.
pages.brief: Several snakes of many different lengths, patterns, and colors appear nearby with no limbs, one in the ocean, one in a tree, and one on land, clearly showing how reptiles also adapt in unusual ways.

pages.text: Where Snakes Live Snakes live almost everywhere except Antarctica. Some places don’t have any snakes. Snakes do not live in the wild on islands such as Ireland, New Zealand, and Iceland. Some snakes in the wild may live up to twenty-five years. Biggest and Smallest The largest snake is the green anaconda. A full-grown green anaconda can be close to 10 meters (33 ft.) long and weigh more than 230 kilograms (507 lb.). One of the smallest snakes is the thread snake. It is only about 12 centimeters (4 in.) long.
pages.brief: A full-grown giant green anaconda lies coiled in a natural setting, while a very tiny thread snake rests nearby; the two snakes together clearly show the overall biggest and smallest sizes described in this book.

pages.text: Snake Traits Like all reptiles, snakes are cold-blooded. Their body temperature changes as the temperature around them changes. If a snake needs to warm up, it lies in the sun. If it needs to cool down, it rests in the shade. Snakes become much less active in winter. Some snakes that live through cold winters find a place underground or beneath a rock pile to stay warm. Another way snakes stay warm is by looping around each other to share body heat.
pages.brief: A snake lies stretched out in bright sunlight to warm up, while another rests in cool shade; nearby, snakes loop around each other in a shared coil, and one slips beneath a rock pile for warmth.

pages.text: Snakes have a long backbone with ribs. Their backbone is made up of many separate bones. Because of this, they can move in many different ways. A snake’s body is covered in scales. The scales protect it. They also help keep the snake dry. The scales grow from the snake’s skin. Some snakes’ scales are colorful. Other scales help them blend in with their surroundings. Since snakes have no arms or legs, they use their scales and muscles to move. The scales on their belly tightly grip the surface beneath them. Their muscles help them move from side to side, or slither, along the ground. Some snakes even use their muscles and scales to climb trees.
pages.brief: A snake slithers smoothly across the ground, its colorful scales catching the light; nearby, another uses its muscles and belly scales to climb up a tree trunk, showing how it moves without arms or legs.

pages.text: Snake scales look like a single sheet of skin. Snakes don’t really shed skin. Instead, they shed the outer layers of their scales. Snakes may shed up to four times per year. This is called molting. During molting, a snake rubs against a hard object such as a rock or log. Rubbing helps its skin stretch and split. Then the snake crawls out and leaves it behind. Snakes shed for several reasons. Young snakes shed more often than older snakes because they outgrow the skin faster. Unlike other animals, snakes’ skin does not stretch as they grow. Another reason snakes shed is to get rid of parasites that may grab on to their old skin.
pages.brief: A snake rubs its body against a rough rock, its old outer layer of scales splitting and peeling; nearby, a clear dry shed snake skin lies left behind on the ground beside a fallen log.

pages.text: Scales also protect a snake’s eyes. Unlike many animals, snakes do not have eyelids. Instead, each eye is covered with a clear scale that protects it from drying out. Because of this, snakes can’t blink. Snakes do not have ears you can see. Instead, sound passes through the jawbone to the inner ear, which sends a signal to the snake’s brain. Snakes have developed a different way to hear sounds with this method.
pages.brief: A close view of a snake's head shows its eye covered by a clear scale and no eyelids; the snake's jaw rests against the ground, suggesting sound passing through the jawbone to its inner ear.

pages.text: Another important feature of a snake is its tongue. A snake smells with its tongue. Its forked tongue picks up scents from the air. Scent particles stick to the tongue. The snake then pulls its tongue back into its mouth. When its tongue touches the roof of its mouth, a special organ helps to identify the scent. Some snakes are able to sense the heat of animals nearby. Pits near the snake’s eyes can sense the air temperature. This kind of sensing helps these snakes judge distances so they can hunt for prey in the dark.
pages.brief: A close-up shows a snake flicking out its forked tongue to pick up scents from the air; the tongue nears its mouth, and small pits near its eyes are visible as it hunts in the dark.

pages.text: Hunting and Eating Snakes are carnivores, or meat eaters. They eat other animals in one of three ways. Some snakes use venom when biting their prey. Other snakes, called constrictors, squeeze their prey to death before swallowing it. Some snakes grab their prey with their jaws and swallow it alive. Most snakes’ upper and lower jaws are loosely connected. As a result, a snake can spread its jaws and open its mouth wide enough to swallow large objects. Snakes’ teeth are mainly made for catching and holding prey. Their fangs and other teeth curve backward, which pushes food toward their throat. They push their breathing tube out of their mouth so they can breathe as they swallow their prey whole. Snakes use strong muscles to move the prey into the stomach and intestines. Strong stomach acids turn the prey into liquid so the snake can digest it easier.
pages.brief: A snake with its jaws stretched wide begins to swallow a large prey whole, its backward-curving teeth holding the meal; nearby, another snake wraps its body tightly around prey as a constrictor on the ground.

pages.text: How Snakes Are Born Most snakes that live in cold areas mate in the late spring or early summer. Snakes that live in warmer areas may mate at any time of year. The male snake usually leaves afterward. About two-thirds of all female snakes lay eggs in a safe place and then leave. Baby snakes grow inside the eggs. Most of them have sharp teeth that they use to cut through the egg to hatch. Once a baby snake leaves the egg, it must face many dangers and survive on its own. Some female snakes hold their eggs inside their body until they hatch. Then they give birth to live babies.
pages.brief: A female snake lays eggs in a safe hidden place and leaves; inside one egg, a baby snake with sharp teeth is ready to cut through the shell, while another female gives birth to live babies nearby.

pages.text: Venomous Snakes Venom is a dangerous substance. Venom comes from the fangs on a snake’s jaws. Venom is made in sacs behind a snake’s eyes. Some fangs are hollow so the venom can flow through them from these sacs.
pages.brief: A close view of a venomous snake's head in the wild shows its fangs and the sacs behind its eyes where dangerous venom is made; its mouth opens slightly to reveal small clear hollow fangs.

pages.text: Snakes use venom to defend and attack. Snakes usually inject more venom when they are defending themselves. The venom paralyzes their prey. Some inject venom and let the prey go. Then they track the prey until it dies. Other snakes use their teeth or body to hold on to prey until it dies. Then they eat it. Venom versus Poison Although commonly confused, venom and poison are not the same thing. Poison is absorbed through the skin, eaten, or breathed in, while venom is injected into the victim by means of a bite or sting.
pages.brief: A snake bites prey and then follows its trail through the undergrowth, waiting for the injected venom to paralyze it; nearby, another snake holds prey with its body until it stops moving before eating it.

pages.text: Conclusion Snakes are among the animal kingdom’s strongest hunters. They have survived in most places all over the world. Their senses have adapted to the natural world in many ways. Snakes are fascinating animals that play an important role in our environment.
pages.brief: Several snakes hunt and rest quietly in different natural surroundings, from bright sunlight to cool shadow, each one showing how their senses and bodies have adapted to survive in most places around the wide world.

books.title: Bison Came Back
books.art_why: Keyword check indicates drawing; the book covers 1800s hunts and past events where real photos of the scenes are impossible.

pages.text: In Bison Came Back readers will learn what bison are, why North American bison nearly became extinct, and what changes helped their population to bounce back.
pages.brief: A wide grassland scene with a herd of shaggy bison grazing and calves beside the adults, heads down in the grass under a broad sky. Distant hills and open plains stretch behind them, suggesting the great beasts of North America and their return.

pages.text: Great Beasts Bison are the biggest animals in North America. They weigh up to 2,000 pounds (907 kg)—almost half as much as a car. They can run 35 miles (56 km) per hour.
pages.brief: A huge bull bison stands squarely on short prairie grass, its massive humped shoulders and shaggy dark coat filling the frame. Behind it another bison runs at full speed, legs stretched, dust kicking up, showing how fast such a heavy animal can move.

pages.text: Although they are big, fast, and strong, bison almost went extinct. People nearly wiped them out by hunting too many.
pages.brief: Bison gallop across open plains, strong and fast, while a line of hunters with rifles kneels in the grass at a distance, aiming. Empty prairie and a few fallen shapes show that too many were being killed, nearly wiping the animals out.

pages.text: People changed their ways just in time. They stopped the big hunts and protected land where bison live. Bison bounced back. Today, there are about a half million bison in North America. If you visit a place such as Yellowstone National Park, you can see them for yourself. Bison or Buffalo? North American settlers often called the shaggy beasts buffalo. Many people still do. In fact, buffalo are a different animal from bison. Buffalo live in Africa and Asia and have no hump. Their heads are smaller, too. However, “buffalo” has become a common name for bison in North America.
pages.brief: A bison herd grazes in a protected Yellowstone meadow while a few visitors watch quietly from a path. Beside them, a humped bison stands next to a smaller-headed, hump-less buffalo, making clear they are different animals that people often confuse.

pages.text: The Great Plains CANADA UNITED STATES MEXICO Millions Turns to Thousands Once, there were around thirty million bison in North America. They lived in large herds, mostly on the Great Plains.
pages.brief: An illustrated map view of North America shows the broad Great Plains stretching from Canada through the United States into Mexico, with countless bison dotted across it in enormous herds, packed shoulder to shoulder as far as the eye can see.

pages.text: They were an important animal for many Native American people. Not only did bison provide food, but their hides were used for clothing and shelter. Native Americans also made bison bones into tools. They used all parts of a bison. For many years, Native Americans lived along with bison. They hunted what they needed but always left enough for herds to stay big.
pages.brief: A Native American family works outside cone-shaped tipis on the plains. People dry strips of bison meat, scrape a hide, and shape tools from bone, while a herd of bison grazes nearby, showing how every part of the animal was used.

pages.text: As settlers moved into the western United States in the 1800s, more bison were hunted. Bison were often killed for sport or for their hides, which were sold. As railroads spread across the West, they brought more hunters. Sometimes thousands of bison were killed in a single day. The U.S. government also killed bison as a way to drive Native Americans off the land. Sadly, by 1889, there were only about one thousand bison left.
pages.brief: Hunters with rifles stand beside a railroad track crossing the plains, wagons loaded with bison hides behind them. Fallen bison lie on the grass, and a distant herd scatters, showing the heavy hunting that left only about one thousand animals by 1889.

pages.text: New Help For years, few people did anything about the bison killing. Some bison were sent to zoos and ranches to protect them. Over time, laws were passed to protect bison in other places. Yellowstone National Park, formed in 1872, became a safe place for bison. People could not hunt them there.
pages.brief: Bison stand safely in a fenced zoo enclosure and on a ranch pasture, while beyond them the wide Yellowstone landscape holds another small herd. A simple boundary fence and open protected land suggest the laws and safe places created to help the animals.

pages.text: In the early 1900s, people shipped bison from East Coast zoos back out West. In 1913, fourteen were brought by train from New York to Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota. Several hundred wild bison live on that land today.
pages.brief: A train car sits on tracks at the edge of a South Dakota prairie. Workers guide bison down a ramp from the car onto the grass of Wind Cave National Park, while a small group of bison already stands in the distance.

pages.text: By 1916, there were just twenty-three bison in Yellowstone, but people shipped more there, too. The bison had plenty of room to roam, and soon their numbers began to grow. Today, there are several thousand bison in Yellowstone.
pages.brief: A broad Yellowstone valley opens up with a meadow and a winding river. Bison roam freely across the grass in small groups, some grazing, some walking, with plenty of open room around them and forested hills rising behind.

pages.text: People in other places also helped bison bounce back. Bison live today on ranches, on the National Bison Range in Montana, and on other government land.
pages.brief: Bison graze on a fenced ranch pasture, and beyond a low ridge more bison stand on rolling Montana grassland. Wide open government land stretches behind them, showing the different places where people helped the animals live.

pages.text: Wonderful Sights Like thousands of other wild animals, bison almost went extinct. There will probably never be as many bison as there once were, but at least they still exist.
pages.brief: A small group of bison stands on a grassy hill in soft evening light, shaggy backs outlined against the sky. Open plains fall away below them, quiet and empty, showing a wild animal that almost disappeared but still exists.

pages.text: Today, bison are easy to spot at a place such as Yellowstone. They love to roll around in the dirt. Sometimes one lets out a great, loud snort. They swim across rivers and run across the land, wild and free. It’s a wonderful sight to see.
pages.brief: At Yellowstone, one bison rolls on its back in a dusty wallow, legs in the air. Another lets out a loud snort, breath misting, while two more wade across a river and others run across the open land, wild and free.

books.title: Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai'i
books.art_why: The book covers Hawai'i's history and traditional hula, including ancient and 1800s scenes best shown in illustration.

pages.text: Hawai i For much of Hawai’i’s history, Hawaiian people did not have a written language and relied on the practice of hula to keep their stories alive. In the 1820s, however, hula was banned. Hawai’i’s history and stories were in danger of disappearing forever with the arrival of Christian.
pages.brief: Hawaiian people practice hula together, moving in rhythm as they keep their stories alive. In the distance, Christian missionaries arrive in the 1820s, and the scene suggests hula being banned. A new form of hula later appears as interest in traditional Hawaiian culture returns.

pages.text: Coming to Hawai‘i The dancers are excited to begin. They have joined a hula school and have danced for many months. Soon, they hear the beat of a drum. Their hula teacher starts to chant in Hawaiian. Now the dancers move together. Their legs sway in rhythm, and their arms move in smooth gestures. At times, they chant along, adding their voices to the story. They are doing hula, a special kind of dance created by their ancestors. They are keeping hula alive today.
pages.brief: Inside a hula school, excited dancers stand ready to begin. Their hula teacher chants in Hawaiian near a drum, and the dancers move together, legs swaying in rhythm and arms making smooth gestures. Some dancers chant along, adding their voices to the story as they keep hula alive.

pages.text: Hawai‘i was settled by Polynesian people around 1200 ce. They traveled 2,600 miles (4,184 km) from the island of Tahiti in the South Pacific Ocean. For most of Hawai‘i’s history, its people did not have a written language. Instead, storytellers told tales with chants and songs. Music and dance added rhythm and drama to these stories. This helped Hawaiian people remember important events in their history. Hawai‘i is the only U.S. state that is made up entirely of islands. Each of its eight main islands was created by at least one volcano. Some traditional Hawaiian stories told about the volcanoes that created the islands.
pages.brief: Polynesian people arrive on the Hawaiian Islands after traveling 2,600 miles from Tahiti in the South Pacific Ocean. A volcano rises behind them. Storytellers chant tales with songs while dancers add rhythm and drama, helping Hawaiian people remember important events from their history.

pages.text: Ancient Hula Traditional Hawaiian storytellers spoke of their ancestors. They told tales about love, war, and Hawaiian gods. They made up songs for important events. Dancers chanted along and danced, often using gestures that helped bring the stories to life. Together, these artists created ancient hula, or hula kahiko (HOO-lah kah-HEE-koh). Hula Skirts Traditionally, hula dancers did not wear grass skirts. Both men and women wore skirts or loincloths made from kapa cloth. Kapa cloth was made from tree bark.
pages.brief: Ancient hula dancers chant and move with gestures that bring stories of ancestors, love, war, and Hawaiian gods to life. The dancers wear skirts or loincloths made from kapa cloth, which comes from tree bark. Storytellers and singers create songs for important events as the dancers perform.

pages.text: Hula Evolves Some modern experts believe that this special dance style started as simple swaying and chanting along with storytellers. In modern hula, most steps are done with knees slightly bent. This lets dancers sway their hips easily. The hips and feet keep the rhythm. The upper body stays straight, appearing to float above the swaying hips. Over time, dancers began to use their arms to make gestures. These gestures described the words in the songs or chants. The dancers’ feelings showed on their faces. Hula teachers taught their students that “the eyes follow the hands.” That way, the dancers became storytellers, too!
pages.brief: Modern hula dancers bend their knees slightly and sway their hips while keeping their upper bodies straight. Their arms make gestures that describe the words in the songs, and their feelings show on their faces. A hula teacher reminds them that the eyes follow the hands.

pages.text: In both ancient and modern hula, every part of the body dances. Hula dancers chant and also create other sounds that become part of the act. They jump, stomp, and slap the ground. These gestures add sound and rhythm to the dance. Hula Gestures.
pages.brief: Hula dancers use every part of the body. They chant, jump, stomp, and slap the ground, creating sounds and rhythm as they move. Their gestures add meaning and beat to the dance in both ancient and modern hula.

pages.text: Strangers Arrive For a while, hula was not allowed in Hawai‘i. The first people from Europe, led by the British explorer Captain James Cook, came to Hawai‘i in 1778. They didn’t stay, but they told the world about the islands. In the 1820s, white Christians from the United States came to Hawai‘i. They wanted Hawaiian people to stop practicing their traditional beliefs and become Christians, too. Because hula was a way to tell stories about Hawaiian gods, they thought it was wrong. The queen of Hawai‘i at the time became a Christian and banned hula in 1830. Then, hula could only be done in secret.
pages.brief: Captain James Cook and European sailors arrive in Hawai'i in 1778. Later, white Christians come from the United States, and the Hawaiian queen becomes a Christian. In 1830 she bans hula, so dancers must practice the dance in secret.

pages.text: King David For the next fifty years, hula was not allowed in Hawai‘i. King David, who ruled from 1874 to 1891, saw that the was changing the country. As people came to Hawai‘i from other places, some Native Hawaiian people felt that their culture was being erased. King David wanted Hawaiian people to feel proud of their culture. He ignored the ban and invited hula dancers to his court. He said, “Hula is the language of the heart, therefore the heartbeat of the Hawaiian people.” King David was famous for his love of hula. During his rule, more than three hundred ancient hula chants and songs were written down and saved.
pages.brief: King David rules from 1874 to 1891 and sees Hawaiian culture being erased as people arrive from other places. He invites hula dancers to his court and ignores the ban. More than three hundred ancient hula chants and songs are written down and saved during his rule.

pages.text: Hard Times Although King David helped bring hula back to Hawaiian culture, its people would continue to face tough times. People from other lands brought new diseases that killed thousands of Native Hawaiian people. More than three hundred thousand Hawaiian people lived on the islands before 1780. By 1890, there were less than forty thousand. Then, in 1898, Hawai‘i became a U.S. territory. With the loss of so many people and the land itself, how could hula live on?
pages.brief: New diseases brought by people from other lands kill thousands of Native Hawaiian people. A large population before 1780 shrinks to less than forty thousand by 1890. In 1898, Hawai'i becomes a U.S. territory, and a hula dancer stands alone, wondering how hula can live on.

pages.text: A New Style of Hula During the early 1900s, many new people came to Hawai‘i. They became interested in hula. A new, modern style of hula, called hula ‘auana (HOO-lah ow-AH-nah), was born. Hula ‘auana used Western- style music instead of chants. It also added new sounds such as the ukulele.
pages.brief: In the early 1900s, many new people come to Hawai'i and become interested in hula. A modern style called hula 'auana is born, using Western-style music instead of chants. Musicians play new sounds, including the ukulele, while dancers perform.

pages.text: Hula ‘auana songs still told stories but focused less on the meaning of the words than hula kahiko. Modern hula was more about the music and gestures, although the words and the dance were still connected.
pages.brief: Hula 'auana dancers perform with music and gestures, telling stories while focusing less on the meaning of the words than hula kahiko. The dance is more about the music and gestures, though the words and the dance remain connected.

pages.text: Hawai‘i Reborn In 1959, Hawai‘i became the fiftieth U.S. state. The 1960s and 1970s marked a new interest in traditional Hawaiian culture. Hawaiian people wanted to bring back the culture that existed in Hawai‘i before people from other places arrived. Some people started studying the Hawaiian language. They learned about ancient hula chants and songs. They also learned to dance hula kahiko.
pages.brief: In 1959, Hawai'i becomes the fiftieth U.S. state. During the 1960s and 1970s, Hawaiian people want to bring back traditional culture. Some study the Hawaiian language and learn ancient hula chants and songs, practicing hula kahiko together.

pages.text: Today, the best hula dancers in the world go to Hawai‘i each spring. They gather to dance at a festival on the Big Island. The hula contest at the festival began in 1971. It is known as the “Olympics of Hula.” It has both hula kahiko and hula ‘auana contests to show how hula has changed over time. Many Native Hawaiian people—and others who care about Hawaiian culture—have started learning about hula again. This interest has helped the ancient stories of Hawai‘i stay alive. Hula lovers are making sure that the “heartbeat of the Hawaiian people” is still strong today.
pages.brief: Best hula dancers from around the world gather in Hawai'i each spring for a festival on the Big Island. The contest, begun in 1971, includes hula kahiko and hula 'auana. Native Hawaiian people and others learn hula again, keeping ancient stories alive.

books.title: The Science of Hiccups
books.art_why: Real children, animals, and body science can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: Hiccup Help You just finished lunch and—hic!— uh-oh. You drank a fizzy drink, and now— hic!—you have the hiccups! Your friends try to help. “Hold your breath!” says one. “Drink a glass of water upside down!” suggests another. “We have a spelling quiz today!” shouts a third.
pages.brief: A photo shows a school-age child at a lunch table just after eating, one hand at the mouth mid-hiccup, with a fizzy drink nearby. Three friends lean in around the table, each offering help with eager faces in a bright cafeteria.

pages.text: “What?” you ask. “Not really,” your friend tells you. “I was just trying to scare the hiccups away!” You try a few tricks, but nothing works. Eventually, the hiccups go away on their own. Usually, hiccups are no big deal, and they come and go quickly. However, many people are curious about hiccups. Some have been trying for years to understand hiccups. They want to know what hiccups are, where they come from, and how to get rid of them. Do You Know? Some people are unlucky enough to have hiccups for months or even years! Jack O’Leary made headlines in 1956 when his hiccups ended after eight years. By that time, he had received more than one hundred thousand letters from people around the country suggesting cures.
pages.brief: A photo shows the child looking puzzled at a friend in a classroom. The friend has a playful, teasing expression after trying to scare away the hiccups. In a small corner scene, a 1950s man sits with stacks of letters from people suggesting cures.

pages.text: What Are Hiccups? A hiccup is a muscle spasm, or twitch. The muscle that twitches is called the diaphragm. You use your diaphragm to breathe. Your diaphragm sits below your lungs and stretches across the bottom of your rib cage. Nerves carry signals from your brain to your diaphragm. To breathe in, your brain tells the diaphragm to tighten. When your diaphragm tightens, it moves downward, which pulls air into your lungs. When your brain tells your diaphragm to relax again, the muscle moves up to push air back out of your lungs.
pages.brief: A realistic medical cutaway of a child's upper body shows the brain, nerves leading to the diaphragm, lungs above it, and the rib cage around them. The diaphragm stretches across the bottom of the rib cage, tightened downward as air flows into the lungs.

pages.text: Breathing in Hiccupping Breathing out During a hiccup, your brain sends a signal to your diaphragm to suddenly jerk downward. Your diaphragm pulls a quick gasp of air into your lungs, and flaps in your throat slam shut. That is why you make a sudden “hic!” sound. Hiccups get their name from this sound.
pages.brief: A photo-realistic view of a child during a hiccup, mouth open in a quick gasp and one hand at the throat. A realistic cutaway beside the child shows the diaphragm jerking downward and flaps in the throat closing, explaining the sudden sound.

pages.text: The spasm can be strong enough to make your whole body jerk. Sometimes, if you have a full stomach, it can even be painful. However, hiccups are not harmful. Take a Breath Have you ever heard of “getting the wind knocked out of you”? Your diaphragm is involved when this happens, too. If you get hit hard in the chest or back, your diaphragm can spasm for a few seconds. The spasm makes it hard to breathe. Soon, your diaphragm relaxes, and you can breathe again.
pages.brief: A photo shows a child mid-hiccup with the whole body jerking and a hand pressed to a full stomach, face uncomfortable but not harmed. Nearby, another child holds a hand to the chest after a hard bump, showing how a diaphragm spasm can briefly make breathing hard.

pages.text: What Causes Hiccups? Hiccups can seem to start for no reason. They might happen when you eat too much or too quickly. Many people get them from eating spicy foods or having fizzy drinks. We know some things about when people might get hiccups, however, we do not know exactly why people get them. Hiccups seem to have no purpose. Scientists have come up with a few theories, or ideas, though. Scientists have found that other animals get hiccups, too. Most that do are mammals. Mammals are animals that drink milk from their mother when they are young. Hiccups are more common in baby mammals, which could be a clue.
pages.brief: A photo shows children eating too quickly at a table with spicy food and fizzy drinks, one child starting to hiccup. Nearby, a mother mammal nurses her young, and a small mammal baby hiccups, hinting that hiccups are common in baby mammals.

pages.text: Baby mammals, humans, need help burping. A burp is how the body gets rid of extra air in the stomach. It can be hard for babies to burp while drinking their mother’s milk. Hiccups may be a way for young mammals to burp. Scientists got another idea from looking at amphibians. These animals include frogs, which breathe water when they are young and air when they are adults. At one stage of growth, amphibians have two different ways to breathe. They can use their lungs to breathe air, or they can breathe water through gills. Do You Know? Babies can even hiccup before they are born! Scientists think it happens as a baby’s lungs, diaphragm, and nerves develop and begin working.
pages.brief: A photo shows a human baby being patted to help burp after feeding, with a parent holding the baby upright. Beside them, a frog sits half in water and half on land, with a realistic view of its young form breathing underwater and its adult form breathing air.

pages.text: When they breathe water, their brain has to send a signal so they don’t breathe water into their lungs. This is similar to the signal the human brain sends during a hiccup. Hiccups may be a sign that the brain is reminding itself how to breathe correctly. Scientists have not yet proven either of these theories. We may never know exactly what hiccups are for. They may not even have a real purpose—maybe they are simply an odd accident in our bodies.
pages.brief: A realistic cutaway of a young frog underwater shows gills and lungs, with a signal pathway from the brain keeping water out. A human child nearby hiccups, suggesting the brain may be reminding itself how to breathe correctly.

pages.text: How Do I Get Rid of Hiccups? Getting rid of hiccups is another mystery. Everyone seems to have his or her own hiccup cure. Sometimes they work, and sometimes they don’t. A hiccup cure that seemed to work last week may not work today. No one has found a cure that works all the time for everyone. However, the most common cures have a few things in common.
pages.brief: A photo shows several people trying different hiccup cures, one holding their breath and one drinking water, while another looks unsure. Their faces show that some cures seem to work while others do not, and no single cure helps everyone.

pages.text: Some cures change your breathing pattern. For example, you might hold your breath or breathe into a paper bag. These methods build up a gas called carbon dioxide in your body. When you have too much carbon dioxide, your body works harder to breathe it out. Your brain tells the diaphragm to relax so it can get rid of the carbon dioxide.
pages.brief: A photo shows a child holding their breath and another breathing into a paper bag. A realistic cutaway view shows carbon dioxide building up in the body, making the body work harder to breathe it out and telling the diaphragm to relax.

pages.text: Other cures distract you. You might try a tricky task, like drinking water from the opposite side of the glass. When you try to breathe or swallow in a different way, the signals between your brain and diaphragm may get confused. Your body may “forget” to hiccup while it tries to do the task. Getting scared works the same way—you get distracted from hiccups. These kinds of hiccup cures may not work forever. Your body learns how to do the tricky task or doesn’t get scared so easily. It becomes harder to distract your brain.
pages.brief: A photo shows a child trying to drink water from the opposite side of a glass, concentrating hard, while another child jumps out to scare them. The tricky task and the surprise distract the brain, confusing signals between brain and diaphragm so the body may forget to hiccup.

pages.text: Unsolved Mystery Hiccups are harmless, but they can be annoying. People have always gotten hiccups, but they are still a scientific mystery. Maybe one day you will be the one to solve the mystery and discover the cure!
pages.brief: A photo shows a child smiling and touching their chest after a bout of harmless but annoying hiccups. The child looks thoughtful and determined, as if wondering about the unsolved mystery and dreaming of discovering the cure one day.

books.title: The Terry Fox Story
books.art_why: A named famous person’s life story is shown in cartoon style.

pages.text: On April 12, 1980, Terry Fox began the Marathon of Hope, an ambitious endeavor to run across Canada in order to raise funds for cancer research. Diagnosed with a rare.
pages.brief: Terry Fox runs along a Canadian road with a determined, hopeful expression, beginning the Marathon of Hope. The wide landscape suggests a long journey across Canada to raise funds for cancer research after his early diagnosis.

pages.text: A Journey Begins Terry Fox was born in 1958 in Winnipeg, Canada. As a young boy, he loved to play sports and games that went on for days. Terry was serious about finishing any project, no matter how long it took. As a child, he loved sports of all kinds. He played baseball and soccer with his little brother, Darrell, and his best friend, Doug Alward. Terry earned a spot on his eighth-grade basketball team, but it wasn’t easy. He was not very tall and not a very good player. Still, through lots of hard work, Terry made the team.
pages.brief: Young Terry Fox plays baseball and soccer with his little brother, Darrell, and best friend, Doug Alward. He works hard at basketball practice, determined to make his eighth-grade team even though he is not tall or a natural star.

pages.text: High School and Beyond Terry kept getting better at basketball while playing for his high school. In his senior year, he shared an Athlete of the Year award with his buddy Doug. Terry also got good grades in school. He wasn’t sure what he wanted to be in the future, but he knew he wanted to keep playing basketball. He went to college at Simon Fraser University, which had the best basketball team in British Columbia. Making the team would take more hard work, but that was just fine with Terry.
pages.brief: Terry Fox plays basketball for his high school, sharing an Athlete of the Year award with his friend Doug. He earns good grades and later joins Simon Fraser University, where he hopes to make the college's strong basketball team through more hard work.

pages.text: Things Crash Terry earned a spot on the team, but then his life started to change. In November of his first year at college, he crashed his car. Terry wasn’t hurt badly in the crash, but his knee felt sore. He didn’t tell anyone about the pain. He thought his knee was hurting from basketball practice. By late winter, however, he was limping. His mother took him to the doctor. The news was not what they expected. The source of Terry’s leg pain was a rare form of cancer. The cause was unknown, but Terry had a type of cancer that could spread quickly and be deadly.
pages.brief: Terry Fox stands beside his damaged car after a crash, then limps into a doctor's office with his mother. The doctor explains that a rare, fast-spreading cancer is the source of the pain in his knee.

pages.text: What Is Cancer? Cancer is the name for a group of diseases that cause a person’s body cells to grow out of control. The disease can start almost anywhere—in bones or even blood. Then, cancer cells can spread throughout the body, creating lumps called tumors. Cancer is the second-leading cause of death around the world.
pages.brief: Inside a human body, cells multiply out of control in bone and blood, forming lumps called tumors. A wide view of the world suggests cancer's serious reach as the second-leading cause of death around the world.

pages.text: Terry was angry and fearful when he first heard the news. He went through many different feelings as he began treatment. He moved into the hospital, and his right leg was removed above the knee. Doctors hoped this would keep the cancer from spreading. No one could say for sure, however, that the cancer wouldn’t return. Terry had to learn how to walk using a prosthetic leg. Months of cancer treatments followed. The treatments weakened his body and caused his hair to fall out. In the hospital, Terry met other people who were being treated for cancer. He realized their experiences were similar to his.
pages.brief: Terry Fox lies in a hospital bed after his right leg is removed above the knee, his face showing anger and fear. He learns to walk with a prosthetic leg, loses his hair during treatment, and meets other cancer patients whose experiences feel similar to his.

pages.text: An Athlete’s Life Terry discovered he could still play sports, though often in new ways. He played wheelchair basketball. To strengthen his body, he trained hard like he always had before. Next, Terry tried running, which was awkward at first with a prosthetic leg. Soon, however, he got the hang of it and began regular training. At his first race, Terry came in last. Still, he felt happy. He had learned that he could do the things he had always loved.
pages.brief: Terry Fox plays wheelchair basketball, trains hard, and tries running with his prosthetic leg. At first the running is awkward, but he improves with regular practice; after finishing last in his first race, he feels happy to do what he loves.

pages.text: A Plan Unfolds Like other cancer survivors, Terry hoped that his cancer would never return. He came up with a plan to help in the search for a cure for the disease. He decided to run across Canada. As he ran, people could give money for cancer research. A huge run such as this one was a lot to take on. But Terry knew that his idea could help a good cause and he carefully planned the trip. He would call his run the Marathon of Hope. His friend Doug would go along with him, driving a van. On April 12, 1980, the Marathon of Hope began in St. John’s, Newfoundland, in eastern Canada.
pages.brief: Terry Fox plans the Marathon of Hope, a run across Canada to raise money for cancer research. His friend Doug drives a van alongside as Terry begins in St. John's, Newfoundland, on April 12, 1980, carefully prepared for the huge challenge.

pages.text: Running Across Canada The run was hard from the start. The days were long, and the weather was freezing cold. At rest breaks, Terry and Doug huddled in the van, making snacks. The narrow country roads Terry ran on were dangerous to share with drivers. Every day Terry’s legs hurt, and he quickly grew sunburned. Sometimes, Terry showed up in a town no one was there to meet him. Other times, lined the streets to cheer him.
pages.brief: Terry Fox runs along narrow country roads in freezing cold, his legs hurting and skin sunburned. At rest breaks he and Doug huddle in the van making snacks. Sometimes no one meets him in a town; other times people line the streets to cheer.

pages.text: Growing Support Terry crossed province after province, running the distance of a marathon each day. Each week of running was draining. Terry’s spirits were lifted when his younger brother, Darrell, joined him on the trip. Growing crowds also made him happy. By late June, dozens of television stations and newspapers were covering his run. The entire country began to follow his journey. In Toronto, Ontario, thousands of people lined the streets as he ran through the city. Money for cancer research was streaming in.
pages.brief: Terry Fox crosses province after province, running a marathon each day. His younger brother Darrell joins the trip, and growing crowds lift his spirits. Television stations and newspapers cover the run, thousands line Toronto's streets, and money for cancer research streams in.

pages.text: Route of Marathon of Hope NORTH AMERICA H u d s o Newfoundland B a START Quebec Prince Edward Ontario Island Canada Nova FINISH Scotia United States Terrible News Then, on September 1, after 5,300 kilometers (3,300 mi.), the Marathon of Hope came to a sudden end. Terry had been feeling sick, and in Thunder Bay, Ontario, he stopped to visit doctors. They discovered that the cancer was back. Terry wanted to keep running, but it was impossible. He had to fly home to get care.
pages.brief: A map of Canada traces the Marathon of Hope from Newfoundland through the provinces toward Thunder Bay, Ontario. There, after 5,300 kilometers, Terry Fox stops to see doctors; they discover the cancer has returned, and he must fly home for care.

pages.text: Terry’s Race Goes On Terry got eight more months of treatment, but on June 28, 1981, he died. Although Terry never finished the Marathon of Hope, the run met his goals. Millions of people learned about the need to find cures for different types of cancer. Terry’s work to fund cancer research didn’t end with his death. Today, the Terry Fox Foundation continues to raise money. Terry’s story still helps new people learn about the cause.
pages.brief: Terry Fox is remembered after his death on June 28, 1981. Although he never finished the Marathon of Hope, millions learned about finding cures for cancer. The Terry Fox Foundation continues his work, raising money and helping new people learn about the cause.

pages.text: Many people take part in yearly Terry Fox runs—one-day events that raise money for cancer research. These runs have taken place in Canada and countries all over the world. So far, the foundation has raised more than 800 million dollars to fund cancer research. A complete cure for cancer hasn’t been found yet, but huge progress has been made. Terry’s run helped people see the difference a single person can make in the world.
pages.brief: Many people take part in yearly Terry Fox runs, one-day events in Canada and countries around the world. Together they raise money for cancer research; so far more than 800 million dollars has been raised, showing the difference one person can make.

books.title: How Memory Works
books.art_why: Real-world science, brains, students, and medical research can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: How Memory Works is an informational book that details how the brain creates different types of memories. Even though so much about how memory works is still unknown, students will get in-depth explanations on what memory is, learn the parts of the brain that handle memories, and discover ideas about how to improve memory.
pages.brief: A group of students sit in a bright classroom, looking curious and thoughtful as they begin learning about memory. One student touches their head, thinking about the brain, while the others listen and consider the topic.

pages.text: A Quick Experiment Let’s do an experiment. Pay attention to what’s going on around you for just a moment. What can you see, touch, taste, smell, and hear? After you paid attention to your senses, did you notice anything different? You probably did. That’s because our brains are always receiving information from our senses. There is so much information, though, that we can’t possibly pay attention to all of it. Indeed, we only remember a very small amount of the information around us. How does memory work? Scientists have some ideas, but many more questions remain.
pages.brief: A child sits quietly in a classroom, eyes open, paying close attention to the surroundings. The child notices sights, textures, tastes, smells, and sounds, perhaps touching a desk and listening. Other students nearby continue normal activity while the child focuses on sensory details.

pages.text: Types of Memory Scientists often talk about two types of memory: working memory and long-term memory. Working memory is how we deal with information in the moment. The words you’re reading right now and the conversation you just had with a friend are part of your working memory. So is the music you were listening to on the way to school. We use our working memory most of the time.
pages.brief: A student reads a book and listens to music while chatting with a friend, showing working memory in action. In the same bright school setting, the student holds several everyday thoughts at once, with a calm expression that suggests handling information in the moment.

pages.text: Short-term memories make up our working memory, which also includes something called executive attention. This is the process of how our brains filter information into short-term memory. Think about the experiment at the beginning of this book. Even when we’re sitting quietly, our brains can’t handle all the information we receive. Our brains ignore most of the information around us to keep from overloading. The information we do keep in our minds at any one time makes up our short-term memory. Most of us can only hold around three to four thoughts in our short-term memory at once.
pages.brief: A child sits at a desk in a quiet classroom, surrounded by many small sights and sounds. The child’s face is focused as the brain filters information, keeping only a few thoughts in mind. The busy surroundings suggest information being ignored.

pages.text: For example, you might be listening to your teacher and scratching an itch on your arm at the same time. You might think about a few other ideas. Then someone sneezes loudly. What happens? Your attention turns to the person who sneezed. Information only stays in our short- term memory for a few seconds. Once our executive attention gets to work and we start paying attention to something, things change. Our executive attention makes sure that unimportant information doesn’t interrupt the things that we are concentrating on. It also makes sure we pay attention to other important things, such as a sneeze. Your brain may think any loud, sudden noise means danger. If we don’t give information attention, it leaves our memory. The more we pay attention to something, the better chance we have to remember it.
pages.brief: A student listens to a teacher while scratching an itch on an arm. Nearby, another student sneezes loudly, and the first student’s attention turns toward the sound. The classroom scene shows the moment concentration shifts from the teacher to the sudden noise.

pages.text: Long-term memories function differently from working memories. They remain in our minds even when we’re not thinking about them. Scientists think information has to go through three steps to become a long- term memory. First, we learn something. Then, we store it. Later, we retrieve it. We can bring back long-term memories when needed. For example, think about your birthday. The date probably came to mind before you even finished reading the sentence. Maybe other memories, such as your birthday parties, also came to mind. You might have even thought about your family. That’s because our brains connect different pieces of related information.
pages.brief: A child smiles while thinking about a birthday, with the date and party memories coming to mind. Family members appear in the warm memory, connected to the birthday thought. The scene shows how related pieces of information link together in the mind.

pages.text: Memory and Our brains do not process or store memories in a single area. In fact, we often use many parts of our brains to make and keep memories. New technology lets scientists see what parts of the brain become active when we use different kinds of memory. The hippocampus (hih-puh-KAM-puhss) is an important part of the brain concerning memory. People have two hippocampi—one on each side of their brain. Scientists aren’t exactly sure how hippocampi work, but they turn short-term memories into long-term memories. They also help us retrieve long-term memories. I Remember Everything! Can you remember everything you did yesterday? What Can you remember everything you did yesterday? What about what you were doing on November 7 two years ago? about what you were doing on November 7 two years ago? Some people can remember everything. They recall what they Some people can remember everything. They recall what they did and who they were with for almost every day of their life— did and who they were with for almost every day of their life— even as babies. even as babies.
pages.brief: A scientist views brain scans on a screen, showing active areas on both sides of a brain. The image focuses on the hippocampus as an important memory region. Nearby, a student thinks quietly, linking the science to everyday remembering.

pages.text: Unlocking the Mysteries of the Brain Scientists learned a lot about what the hippocampus does through working with a patient, Henry Molaison (MOH-luh- suhn), known as HM. He was born with a disease called epilepsy (EH-puh-lep-see), which affects the brain. Doctors removed part of HM’s brain, including the hippocampus, when he was twenty-seven to try to help him. He got better, but he was no longer able to form some types of long-term memories. For example, HM could learn new motor skills, such as drawing a star in a mirror or walking with crutches. However, he couldn’t remember someone he met minutes before, new words, or songs. In fact, he couldn’t remember any new information about himself or his experiences after the age of sixteen. Scientists studied HM for fifty-five years before he died in 2008. Much of what we know about how memory works is thanks to studies done with him. In fact, HM is one of the most studied people in the history of medicine!
pages.brief: A historical medical scene shows Henry Molaison as a young adult patient with doctors and scientists nearby. Brain scans and a hospital setting suggest the study of his memory after surgery. Researchers observe carefully, reflecting fifty-five years of study.

pages.text: Other parts of our brain become active with muscle memory. We form muscle memory when we repeat a movement over and over again. Eventually, we don’t even have to think about how to do the movement—we just do it.
pages.brief: A person repeats a physical movement again and again, practicing a skill with a focused expression. The repeated motion is shown in a simple setting where the body learns the action. Eventually, the movement becomes automatic, needing no conscious thought.

pages.text: Losing Memory Damage to the brain can cause people to lose their memory. This is called amnesia. They may forget just a few minutes or a long period of time. It depends on how bad the damage is. Sometimes amnesia goes away in days, weeks, or months. Other times, it never goes away. One of the most common diseases that affects memory is called Alzheimer’s (AHLTS-hy-murz). People who have Alzheimer’s lose their memories over time. Most of the people who have the disease are over the age of sixty-five. Scientists don’t know what causes Alzheimer’s. Another part of our brain connects feelings to memory. Strong feelings, such as happiness, sadness, or pride, can make memories last longer. They help make memories clearer. While people remember happy memories, they often recall painful or sad memories more clearly —especially ones they’d rather forget.
pages.brief: An older adult sits quietly with a thoughtful, distant expression, supported by a caring person nearby. Another scene suggests strong feelings linked to memory, with a face showing sadness or happiness. The image conveys memory loss and the lasting strength of emotional memories.

pages.text: Improving Memory Information enters our long-term memory in a few different ways. One way is to repeat something over time. The more you experience something, the better you remember it. It’s also true that the longer the period of time over which you repeat something, the better you’ll remember it. This is why studying every day helps you do better in school. You’ll remember more if you study for one hour a day for five days than five hours in one day.
pages.brief: A student studies at a desk in short daily sessions, repeating the same learning over several days. The calm, focused scene shows one hour of study repeated across five days, rather than a single long stretch.

pages.text: You can also learn by using mnemonic (nih-MON-ik) devices that help you remember information. They connect new information to information you already know or that is easy to remember. One example is “Never eat soggy waffles.” People use this sentence to remember the names and order of the four major directions. The first letter of each word is the same as the first letter of north, south, east, and west. You still need to repeat mnemonic devices over and over to remember the connection. However, they help you remember more with less work. Give it a try! North West East South.
pages.brief: A student smiles while repeating a silly sentence about soggy waffles to recall four major directions. The student gestures toward the space around them, imagining north, south, east, and west. The scene shows a memory trick linking new information to an easy phrase.

pages.text: Mysterious Memory We learn more about memory every year. New technology helps scientists study our brains in action. Yet scientists still don’t really know what memories are or how they are made. They also don’t know how memories move from our working memory to our long-term memory. How we retrieve them is also a mystery. Scientists have ideas about how memory works, but it could be many years before we have clear answers to these mysteries. Whoever discovers how memory works will be remembered far into the future. Could it be you?
pages.brief: A scientist studies brain images on screens in a laboratory, while a student looks upward with curiosity. The scene suggests new technology helping researchers watch brains in action. Open questions remain, and the student’s thoughtful face hints that the next discovery could come from someone young.

books.title: Mysterious Mars
books.art_why: The keyword check calls for drawing, covering ancient sightings and historical Mars missions.

pages.text: Have you ever wondered what makes Mars red? In Mysterious Mars, students will find out why Mars is red and so much more! Students will learn about NASA’s various Mars exploration programs and what scientists know about this fascinating planet so far.
pages.brief: A bright red Mars floats in space beside a small group of students and scientists. NASA spacecraft and exploration machines are shown nearby, hinting at the planet’s mysteries. The scene introduces a journey to learn why Mars is red and what scientists have discovered about it so far.

pages.text: Introduction Long ago, ancient people saw a bright red light in the sky. The Romans named this red light Mars, after their god of war. The name stuck, and we still use it today for the fourth planet in our solar system.
pages.brief: Ancient people stand outdoors at night, gazing at a bright red light in the sky. A Roman figure in armor, like the god of war, stands beside the red planet. The scene shows how the fourth planet got the name Mars.

pages.text: Gazing from Afar Ancient astronomers wondered what made Mars red. Astronomers in the 1800s studied the planet through early telescopes. They found that Mars had polar ice caps just as Earth did. Parts of Mars were also covered with long lines that looked like a web of waterways.
pages.brief: Astronomers in the 1800s peer through early telescopes at Mars in the night sky. On the planet, white polar ice caps gleam, and long lines cross parts of the surface like a web of waterways. The astronomers study these features, wondering what makes Mars red.

pages.text: An Italian astronomer who discovered these lines in 1877 called them channels. Channels are natural waterways. People thought the astronomer said he saw canals. Canals are waterways built by people. The mix-up led people to believe that intelligent beings built canals on Mars! Were the channels on Mars really canals? Had they held water? And why was Mars red? Scientists had many questions about the planet.
pages.brief: An Italian astronomer in 1877 looks through a telescope and points to long lines on Mars. Nearby, people imagine the lines as canals built by intelligent beings. The scene shows the mix-up between natural channels and people-made canals, leaving many questions about water and why Mars is red.

pages.text: Taking a Closer Look In the 1960s, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) began the Mariner missions to answer these questions. The Mariner 4 spacecraft traveled to Mars to take close-up pictures. The pictures showed that the “canals” were canyons.
pages.brief: In the 1960s, a NASA Mariner 4 spacecraft travels through space toward Mars. Close-up pictures reveal the long lines on the planet are canyons, not canals. The spacecraft is shown taking those images while scientists on Earth await answers about the red planet.

pages.text: The Mariner 9 spacecraft showed that Mars had valleys and volcanoes. One of the volcanoes is the largest on any planet in our solar system. It is 26 kilometers (16 mi.) high and 500 kilometers (311 mi.) wide at its base. That’s three times as tall as Mount Everest! Mariner 9 was launched in 1971. It was the first satellite to orbit Mars, and it stayed in orbit for nearly a year. During that time, it collected over seven thousand images, which allowed scientists to map most of the Martian surface.
pages.brief: The Mariner 9 spacecraft orbits Mars in 1971, the first satellite to circle the planet. Below, valleys and a giant volcano stretch across the surface; the volcano is far taller than Mount Everest and very wide at its base. The spacecraft gathers images to map most of Mars.

pages.text: Earth Mars Why is a Mars year almost twice as long as an Earth year? A year is the amount of time it takes a planet to orbit the Sun. Mars is farther away from the Sun than Earth is, so it has a longer distance to travel. Its orbiting speed is also a bit slower than Earth’s. Scientists also learned that the atmosphere on Mars is much thinner than Earth’s. It can’t filter the Sun’s harmful rays the way Earth’s atmosphere can. Mars is also very cold, with an average temperature of −63 ° Celsius (−81 ° F).
pages.brief: Earth and Mars appear side by side in space, with Mars farther from the Sun and moving more slowly along its longer orbit. A thin atmosphere surrounds Mars, unable to filter harmful rays like Earth’s. Mars looks very cold, with an average temperature of −63°C.
